In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾

The address here is general to all of mankind. Usually, the address that calls for faith is general to all people; but when it calls for the implementation of a legal ruling, it says: "O you who have believed."

Therefore He says here: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord...﴾. He intends to draw their attention to the strength of faith. The word ﴿fear your Lord...﴾: taqwa (God-consciousness, fear of God) means that you place between yourself and what I am telling you about a protection, i.e., something that shields you from the punishment which you have no power to bear.

We note that Allah the Exalted says once: ﴿Fear Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:194], and once He says: ﴿so fear the Fire...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24]. Yes, because the meaning ends in one thing. The meaning of ﴿so fear the Fire...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24] is: place between you and it a protection that shields you from it, and this is by doing what is commanded and abandoning what is forbidden.

As for His saying ﴿Fear Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:194]: because Allah the Exalted has attributes of beauty and attributes of majesty. The attributes of beauty are like the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), the Most Compassionate (al-Rahim), the Expander (al-Basit), and the Concealer (al-Sattar), and the attributes of majesty are like the Subduer (al-Qahhar), the Compeller (al-Jabbar), and others of what we fear from.

So place between yourself and the attributes of majesty a protection, for you have no power against His dominance and His seizing, glory be to Him, and the Fire is among the soldiers of Allah and one of the manifestations of His subjugation. Just as we say: "Fear Allah," we say: "Fear the Fire."

In this matter He chose the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), saying: ﴿fear your Lord...﴾ [al-Hajj 22:1], and He did not say: "Fear Allah," because the Lord (Rabb) is the One who undertakes nurture and upbringing. The One who warns you is the One who loves you and gives to you; He is the One who created you, raised you, and cared for you.

So lordship is giving: bringing into existence from nothing and sustaining from nothing; it is more fitting for you to be mindful of Him, because He has bestowed upon you goodness.

As for the attribute of divinity (uluhiyyah), it means obligations and worship, with "do" and "do not do": Allah is the One worshipped and obeyed in what He commands and in what He forbids.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ [al-Hajj 22:1]. Al-zalzalah (convulsion): it is the violent, intense movement that removes things from their stability, as if you wanted to pull out a stake from the ground: first you must shake it and loosen it from its place, until you create room for it in the earth to come out. Whereas if you tried to pull it directly at the beginning, you would find effort and hardship in extracting it; and likewise the dentist does in extracting a molar.

So the meaning of zalzalah is the intense movement that removes things from their places. The Truth, glory be to Him, spoke much about this movement, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:4], ﴿and the mountains are crumbled to crumbling﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:5], ﴿and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:6].

And He says: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake, and the earth discharges its burdens, and man says, "What is wrong with it?" On that Day it will report its news, because your Lord has inspired it.﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:1–5].

So the earthquake here is not an earthquake like what we see of earthly tremors that destroy some houses or even swallow some villages. Those are merely cosmic signs that confirm the truthfulness of the message from Allah and alert you to the great earthquake in the Hereafter. It is a miniature image of what will happen in the Hereafter, so that we are not deceived by our sovereignty in this world, for sovereignty is a gift to us from Allah.

When the earthquake of "Agadir" occurred, you noticed that the animals were agitated and roused minutes before the earthquake, and some of them went out into the open. What kind of announcement is this? And what kind of perception do they have, being beasts in our view that do not understand or perceive?

In that is a sign to the human being who considers himself the lord of the universe: take heed. Had Allah not been your Master, these beasts would have struck you down and destroyed you.

We say: this is not a general earthquake, but a specific earthquake attributed to the earth by revelation from Allah, and by His command, glory be to Him, that it be shaken.

Therefore this earthquake is described as a tremendous thing: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing.﴾ [al-Hajj 22:1]. When you, O human, say: "This is a tremendous thing," it is tremendous by your measure; but the tremendous here is tremendous by the measures of the Truth, glory be to Him. So imagine the awfulness of an earthquake that Allah, glory be to Him, has described as tremendous.

This surah has opened with the convulsion of the Resurrection, because the Truth, glory be to Him, had already said: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:97]. So it must give us here an image of this promise, a summary of what will happen in it, and a miniature image that indicates His capability over the earthquake of the Hereafter, and that the earth has no stability in itself; its stability is by the command and power of Allah. If He wills for it to cease, it ceases.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿And the earth discharges its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:2]:

What we see of volcanoes, of the treasures within the earth's depths, and of wonders falls under this verse. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:6].

Since the Truth, glory be to Him, bestows favor by the ownership of what is beneath the soil, there must be treasures and precious things beneath the soil. We now extract most of the wealth from within the earth, and most wealthy nations depend on buried wealth of petroleum, minerals, mines, gold, etc.

We have previously mentioned that the Truth, glory be to Him, scattered goodness throughout His creation and gave each of them its appropriate time; for provision has a birth in which it appears: ﴿And We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr 15:21].

1 - bassa: crushed it and made it into fine particles. That is, it was crushed intensely. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/66].

The Almighty then says:

﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she was nursing, and every pregnant one will drop her load, and you will see people intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾ (1–2)

Regarding the seeing (ru'yah): we have said that it may be a rational seeing ('ilmiyyah) or a visual seeing (basariyyah). And that which we know is either knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqin), or the eye of certainty ('ayn al-yaqin), or the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin).

Knowledge of certainty is when you are told something by someone you trust, just as reports about a continent by travellers were widely transmitted, which they later named America, and that it has such-and-such. This we call "knowledge of certainty." Then, when you board the aircraft to America and see it and witness what is there, this is "the eye of certainty." Then when you land there and walk around among its streets and buildings, this we call "the truth of certainty."

Therefore, when Allah the Exalted informs the disbelievers that there is punishment in the Fire, this information is true from Allah, so our knowledge of it is "knowledge of certainty." When we see it, this is "the eye of certainty," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾ [At-Takathur].

When its people actually encounter it and taste its heat and blaze — and this is restricted to the people of the Fire — then they know it with the truth of certainty. Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿But if he is of the companions of the right, then, "Peace be upon you," from the companions of the right. And if he is of the deniers and the astray, then is a welcome of boiling water and burning in Hellfire. Indeed, this is the true certainty.﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah 90–95) ﴿So exalt by the name of your Lord, the Most Great.﴾ (96)

As for the meaning of ﴿every nursing mother will be distracted from what she was nursing﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj]: al-dhuhul (distraction) is the turning of a limb away from its true function because of a terror it has seen, so that it becomes occupied with what it has seen and neglects performing its task, just as a servant becomes distracted when he sees a person of awe or greatness, so that what is in his hand falls, for example. Distraction, then, is an involuntary behaviour which may be a distraction from something imposed by emotion, or from something imposed by instinct.

Emotion is like the mother who is distracted from her child. The emotion of motherhood is proportionate to the child's need. In the stage of pregnancy, for example, you find the mother taking care in her walking and her movements, out of fear for the foetus in her womb. This emotion Allah placed in the heart of the mother to preserve the newborn; otherwise it would be exposed to what harms it or ends its life.

Therefore, when they asked the Arab woman which of her children she loved most, she said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers." So according to need, Allah gives the emotion; the pregnant woman's emotion toward her child is strong, and so it is in the stage of nursing.

Look, then, at the nursing mother, and how she is distracted from her infant and turns away from him. What terror is this that occupies her and disables in her the emotion of motherhood and tenderness, and disables even the instinct?

The Qur'an has given us another image in His saying: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his companion and his children.﴾ (Abasa 34–36)

Among the greatness of the Qur'anic style is that the brother is mentioned here before the father and mother. They said: because the parents may be found at a time when one does not see that they are in need of him, nor he in need of them because he has grown up; but the brother contains the hope of help and assistance.

And His saying: ﴿every nursing mother...﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj]:

The word "murdi'ah" comes with a fatha or a kasra on the dad: murdi'ah with a fatha is one whose nature is to nurse and who is fit for this process; whereas murdi'ah with a kasra is one who is actually nursing, now placing her breast in her child's mouth, so she is nursing.

So look, then, at the extent of distraction and preoccupation in such a state.

His saying: ﴿and every pregnant one will drop her load﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj]: After speaking of the nursing mother, the matter is elevated to the pregnant one. It is well known that holding on to the pregnancy is a strong instinct in the mother, even in her bodily formation, for the womb, as soon as the fertilised ovum reaches it, closes around it, as the Glorified said: ﴿And We settle in the wombs what We will for an appointed term...﴾ (Al-Hajj 5)

When the time of birth comes, it opens for it by the power of Allah. This, then, is a matter of instinct beyond the mother's power and without her will. Therefore, the release of this load is evidence of a great terror and a tremendous matter occurring.

Burden is of two kinds: a weight you carry which is other than you, and a weight you carry within yourself. Among the latter is His saying: ﴿And they will bear, on the Day of Resurrection, a burden (himl)﴾ (Taha 101). The hamal (with a kasra on the ha) is the heavy thing that your back cannot bear, whereas hamal with a fatha is a light thing you carry in yourself. In this sense the poet says:

"What the back can bear does not weigh;
The only burden is what the chest contains."

That is: the thing you are able to carry and your back is strong enough for is not a burden; rather the burden is the worry that the chest holds.

Then the Glorified says: ﴿And you will see people intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj]: sukara (intoxicated) means swaying, staggering, like drunkards when wine sways them, tossing them right and left and throwing them to the ground. And whenever their intoxication and their departure from their natural state increases, the kind is severe.

So it will be in the situation of the Resurrection, not from intoxication but from fear, terror and dread: ﴿and they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj].

But from where does this unsteadiness of movement come?

They said: because Allah the Exalted created the limbs, and placed in every limb the instinct of coordination and balance. Anatomists identify in the body particular organs and regions responsible for maintaining the body's balance; when these glands and organs are affected, a person feels dizziness and loses his balance, as when you look from a high place, or travel on the sea, for example.

So this unsteadiness is not from intoxication, but from the terror of what they see; thus a change occurs in the glands and cells responsible for balance, and they sway like someone overcome by wine.

As for His saying: ﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe.﴾ (2) [Al-Hajj]: they have not yet seen the punishment; it is only the coming of the Hour and its terrors that has deprived them of their balance. For whoever believes that the Resurrection will take place in this form believes also that after it there is punishment in Hell. So: the matter is settled, and what we used to deny is now standing before our eyes.

1 – That is: they will be occupied (tashtaghil). Said by Qurtubi. It is also said: they forget; and it is said: they play; and it is said: they are consoled; and the meaning is close. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4536].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 3:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil.﴾

Al-jidal (debate, disputation): it is the exchange between two parties, each of whom wants to support his own opinion and refute the opinion of the other. From it comes the phrase jadal al-khaws or al-habl, meaning twisting one strand over another.

If you reflect on the process of spinning wool or cotton, you will find that it consists of short fibres, not exceeding a few centimetres, yet they make from them a long rope, because they interlace these fibres with one another, so that the end of one fibre lies in the middle of another. In this way it is twisted and spun. And if you want to strengthen this twist, you braid it with another twist. Likewise is debate in ideas: every holder of an idea tries to strengthen his opinion and his argument in order to refute the arguments of others.

Now, His saying, ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah...﴾ [al-Hajj]: how can there be debate about Allah, may He be exalted?

Debate about Allah may concern His existence, as with the atheist who does not acknowledge the existence of a god. Or it may concern His oneness, as with one who associates another god with Allah. Or it may concern the announcement by Allah of an unseen matter, such as the Hour, which some deny and do not believe. All of this is debate about Allah.

As for His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj]: therefore, debate in itself is permissible and lawful, on condition that it proceeds from knowledge and understanding, as He says: ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 125].

Allah, then, does not forbid debate, but He wants it to be conducted in the best manner and in a gentle style. As they say: "Advice is heavy, so do not make it debate, nor send it like a mountain, and do not move a person from what he is accustomed to by means of what he dislikes." Read His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction﴾ [al-Nahl 125].

He, glorified is He, also said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the way that is best﴾ [al-'Ankabut 46].

Therefore, the noble Qur'an teaches the Messenger (ﷺ) a form of debate in His saying: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed, nor will we be questioned about what you do﴾ [Saba' 25].

Look at this elevated debate and this lofty style. In addressing them, He says: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed﴾ [Saba' 25], attributing the crime to Himself. But when He speaks of them, He says: ﴿nor will we be questioned about what you do﴾ [Saba' 25]. He did not say "what you commit" here, so that there would be a contrast between the two states. In this style there is what there is of attracting hearts and inclining them to accept the truth.

When they accused the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of madness, the Qur'an answered them with reason and logic. It asked them: What is madness? Madness is that voluntary movements proceed from the brain without a choice of alternatives. Have you tested Muhammad in any of this? And what is good character (khuluq)? Good character is the straightness of method and conduct on the path of perfection and goodness. Have you seen in Muhammad anything contrary to this?

Therefore He, exalted is He, says in response to them: ﴿Say: I admonish you with one thing: that you stand up for Allah in pairs and singly, then reflect [on] what there is in your companion of madness﴾ [Saba' 46].

How could one who has this upright character and this disciplined conduct in goodness be mad?

When they said, "He is a liar," the Qur'an debated with them: ﴿I have remained among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason?﴾ [Yunus 16]. The message came to him after forty years. Have you heard of him as an orator or a poet? Did he deliver a sermon or a qasida that you preserve as you preserve the qasidas of your poets?

And they said: "It is genius that was in Muhammad." What genius is this that erupts after forty? If you reflect on the geniuses, you will find them in the second or third decade of their lives. How, then, would Muhammad postpone his genius until forty? And who guarantees him life when he sees people falling around him? His father died before he was born, his mother died when he was a suckling infant, and his grandfather died when he was still young.

Thus the Qur'an gives us an example of debate by wisdom and good instruction, debate that proceeds from knowledge of what one says and from understanding of the realities of matters.

Therefore, when al-Sha'bi(3) went to the king of the Romans, the king said to him: "You have in Islam matters that reason does not accept." Al-Sha'bi said: "What in Islam contradicts reason?" He said: "You say that in Paradise there is food that never runs out, and we know that whatever is taken from it again and again must eventually run out. Look at how debate on this issue is conducted."

Al-Sha'bi said: "Tell me, if you had a lamp, and the whole world came and lit its flame from its light, would any of the lamp's light be diminished?" This, then, is elevated debate, at the highest level.

The king of the Romans continued: "How do we eat in Paradise everything we desire without defecating, or without having waste?" We say: "Have you seen the foetus in the mother's womb: does it grow or not? It grows day after day, and this is evidence that it is nourished. Does it have waste? If the foetus had waste, even if it defecated in its placenta, it would die. Therefore, the foetus is nourished with food according to the measure of its growth's need, so that nothing of its food remains."

Then he said: "Where do the souls go after they leave the bodies?" The man answered in general terms: "They go to where they were before they dwelt in you." Then he placed before him a lamp that had light in it, then blew out the lamp, and said to him: "Where did the light go?"

From the debate that came from knowledge and understanding is what happened with the Imam 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, when the companions of Mu'awiya killed 'Ammar ibn Yasir. The Companions in Mu'awiya's ranks grew angry and remembered the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about 'Ammar: "The rebellious group will kill him."(4) They began to leave Mu'awiya's army one after another. 'Amr ibn al-'As went to Mu'awiya and said: "Rumour has spread through the army. If it continues, not a single man will remain with us." Mu'awiya said: "And what is it?" He said: "They say: we killed 'Ammar, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said of him: 'The rebellious group will kill him.'"

Mu'awiya was perplexed and then said: "Tell them: the one who brought him out to fight killed him."(5) That is, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. When this speech reached our master 'Ali, he said: "Tell them: then who killed Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib?" That is, if the matter is as you say, then the Prophet (ﷺ) is the killer of Hamza, because he is the one who brought him out to fight.

This is debate from knowledge. Knowledge may be self-evident knowledge, which is what you believe in without being able to prove it. Or it may be rational, inferential knowledge. And knowledge may come through revelation from Allah, which no one has any part in. We have previously given an example of self-evident truths with a small child who sees his brother sitting beside their father on a chair, for instance. The child comes wanting to sit beside the father himself, so he first tries to remove his brother from the place, pulling and dragging him so that the place is cleared for him.

Here we ask: how did the small child know that a space cannot hold two things? And that nothing can occupy a place unless what is in it leaves first?

These are matters we learned only in our secondary studies, when we came to know the meaning of space and the non-interpenetration of things. A child knows these matters intuitively.

If you reflect on geometric theorems, you will find that every theorem is built upon a previous theorem. So if you want to prove the hundredth theorem, you use the ninetieth theorem, for instance, and so on, until you reach a self-evident principle for which there is no proof.

Thus you can say: every scientific thing in the universe is built upon self-evident truths that need no proof, and you cannot give them a definition. The sky, for example, they say, is "whatever is above you and shades you." So the ceiling is sky, the cloud is sky, the rain cloud is sky, and the sky is sky. Yet the sky does not need such a definition, because when you hear this word ("the sky") you know its meaning intuitively without definition.

These self-evident matters are not subject to debate, because they are clear. If you say to this child, "Sit on your brother," this is not debate, because it is not valid.

As for inferential knowledge, it is that you infer one thing from another. For example, you enter your house and find (a cigarette butt) in the ashtray, and you ask: "Who came to you today?" Or like the Arab man who travelled in the desert and found on the ground the tracks of a camel's hoof and its dung, and he said: "The dung indicates the camel, and the footprint indicates the traveller."

As for the knowledge of revelation, it comes from above, cast by Allah, glorified is He, upon whomever of His servants He wills.

So the one who debates must use one of these three to debate with. If he debates without knowledge, then it is sophistry with no benefit in it.

This verse was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj 3], concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to argue without knowledge about existence, about oneness, about resurrection, and so on.

The verse does not refer to al-Nadr alone, but to everyone who does his deed and goes the way of his kind of debate.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and follows every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Hajj 3]. That is, this debate may arise from a person's own self, or from the whispering of Satan to him, which contradicts the method of Allah, whether he is a devil of mankind or a devil of the jinn.

Therefore, evil deeds, deviations and departure from the method of Allah occur either through whisperings, either from the self that does not cease to oppose, or from Satan who insists upon you until he traps you in his snare.

But we should not make Satan a scapegoat on which to hang all our sins and transgressions. Not every sin is from Satan. Among sins are those that come from the self itself. We have previously said: if Satan is the one who whispers evil, then who whispered to him first? As the poet said: "Iblis, when he went astray, whose Iblis was he?"

There is a difference between disobedience by way of the self and disobedience by way of Satan. Satan wants you disobedient in any way whatsoever, whereas the self wants you disobedient in one specific way from which it does not turn aside. If you divert it to something else, it will not turn, and it refuses you, unless it brings you into that very thing. This is in contrast to Satan: if you refuse him and do not obey him in one disobedience, he turns you to another disobedience, whatever it may be. The important thing is that you disobey. In this way you can distinguish between disobedience from your self and disobedience from Satan.

When one of the scholars was asked: "How do I know whether I am one of the people of this world or of the next?" He said: "This is not a matter for the scholars; it is with you yourself." He asked: "How?" He said: "Look into yourself. If the one who takes charity from you is dearer to you than the one who gives you a gift, know that you are of the people of the next world. And if the gift is dearer to you than charity, then you are of the people of this world."

That is because a person loves whoever builds up for him what he loves. The one who gives you, builds up for you the world that you love, so you love him. Likewise, the one who takes from you builds up for you the next world that you love, so you love him. This is a matter in which Satan has no part.

In another verse, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating book﴾ [Luqman 20].

This verse summarises the three types of knowledge we have discussed. Knowledge refers to self-evident truths, guidance refers to inference, and the illuminating book refers to what has come as revelation from Allah. With these three, debate must be conducted, and "in the way that is best."

The meaning of ﴿rebellious﴾ [al-Hajj 3]: from marada or amrada, like nathara yanthuru (to scatter). Al-marud means defiance and reaching the extreme of corruption. From it come marid, marid and mutamarrid. The marid is one who rises above you.

1 - Abu Malik said, as narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith [al-Durr al-Manthur by al-Suyuti 6/8]. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4537): "He said, i.e., al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: Allah is not able to revive one who has decayed and returned to dust."

2 - That is: stand up sincerely for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without desire or partisanship, so that one of you asks another: "Is there madness in Muhammad?" Then one of you advises another, and each looks into the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) for himself, and if it is unclear to him he asks others about his condition, and reflects upon it. [Said by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3/543].

3 - He is 'Amir ibn Sharahil al-Sha'bi al-Himyari, Abu 'Amr, a narrator from the Successors, proverbial for his memory. Born in the year 19 AH, he grew up and died suddenly in Kufa in the year 103 AH at the age of 84. He was attached to 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, becoming his boon companion and his envoy to the king of the Romans. He was slight and thin, and he is among the trustworthy men of hadith, a jurist and a poet. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 3/251].

4 - From Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Ammar: "The rebellious group will kill you." Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (2916), Book of Afflictions, and by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (447).

5 - From Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm, from his father, who said: When 'Ammar ibn Yasir was killed, 'Amr ibn Hazm entered upon 'Amr ibn al-'As and said: "'Ammar has been killed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The rebellious group will kill him.'" 'Amr ibn al-'As rose in alarm and went back until he entered upon Mu'awiya. Mu'awiya said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "'Ammar has been killed." Mu'awiya said: "'Ammar has been killed, so what?" 'Amr said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The rebellious group will kill him.'" Mu'awiya said to him: "You have been refuted in your urine! Did we kill him? Rather, 'Ali and his companions killed him. They brought him until they threw him between our spears" or he said, "between our swords." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (4/199).

﴿It is decreed concerning him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ (22:4)

That is: God has decreed upon this rebellious devil, and has passed a definite judgment against him, [as it were] "his eye for your eye," as one says. ﴿Whoever takes him as an ally...﴾ (22:4): that is, follows him and goes in his footsteps. ﴿...he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (22:4). "Mislead" and "guide" are opposites, so how can we reconcile them?

The meaning is: he misleads him away from the path of truth and goodness, and guides him to evil. This is because the meaning of guidance (hidayah) is simply indication (dalalah) in general: if you indicate a good thing, it is guidance; and if you indicate an evil thing, it is also guidance.

And consider His saying, glorified and exalted be He:
﴿Gather those who did wrong, along with their companions, and what they used to worship, besides God, and guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ (37:22–23). That is: point them out and take them by the hand to Hell.

And He says in another verse:
﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and did wrong, God would never forgive them, nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, wherein they will abide forever﴾ (4:168–169). As-Sa'ir: it is the blazing fire that neither dies down nor is extinguished.

(1) Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: "By their companions (azwajahum) is meant their like and their equivalents." 'Umar said: "The people of adultery will come with the people of adultery, the people of usury with the people of usury, and the people of wine with the people of wine." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/4].

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop (nutfah), then from a clinging clot ('alaqah), then from a lump of flesh (mudghah), formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for an appointed term. Then We bring you out as a child, then [We let you grow] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age, so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows [something] of every lovely kind (5)﴾:

His saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]:

Ar-raib: doubt. The meaning is: if you are doubting the matter of the Resurrection, then here is the proof of its truth for you: ﴿then indeed We created you from dust...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, the first creation, which is Adam, peace be upon him. As for the majority of people after Adam, they were created from a living drop (nutfah) of a living human.

Whoever follows the verses of the Qur'an finds that the Truthful, glorified and exalted is He, says once about the creation of man: ﴿from dust...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj], and once ﴿from water...(6)﴾ [at-Tariq], and ﴿from clay...(2)﴾ [al-An'am], and ﴿from black mud, moulded (26)﴾ [al-Hijr], and ﴿from clay like pottery (14)﴾ [ar-Rahman]. These are what prompted the orientalists to object to the style of the Qur'an; they say: From which of these things were you created?

This objection arises from a failure to understand the language of the Qur'an. Dust, water, clay, black moulded mud and dry clay are all multiple stages of one thing. When you put water on dust it becomes clay; if you leave the clay until it ferments and its parts mingle with one another so that you cannot distinguish one element in it from another, and when it putrefies and its smell changes, it becomes black moulded mud (hama' masnun); if it dries, it is clay like pottery, and from it God created man and fashioned him and breathed into him of His spirit. So these are stages of one thing, and a thing passing through different stages does not change it.

Then He, glorified is He, spoke of the second creation after Adam, peace be upon him, namely his offspring, and said: ﴿then from a drop...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: The nutfah originally means a drop of sweet water, as the poet said: "Remnants of drops whose clarity the clouds deposited, heavy at the edges, blue at the sides." The blueness of water appears only when it is clear and unmixed. Likewise the nutfah is the essence of essences, because the human body undergoes combustion and metabolism, that is, continual demolition and construction, which results in the emission of various wastes from the body: urine, faeces, sweat, tears and earwax are all wastes resulting from the burning of food inside the body, where the body absorbs the essence of nourishment and conveys it to the blood.

From this essence is extracted the semen of man from which the nutfah is taken; it is therefore the essence of essences in man, and from it conception occurs and the foetus forms, as if the Creator, mighty and majestic, had refined it with this refinement and purified it with this purity, because it would be the origin of His most noble creation, man.

This nutfah descends from man only during intercourse, and it is the most delightful pleasure in the living human's existence. Why? If you reflect on man's other pleasures and delights, such as the pleasure of taste, smell or touch, these are known pleasures limited to a specific human sense; but this pleasure accompanying the emission of semen during this sexual act is an all-encompassing pleasure by which the whole body trembles, and you cannot determine in it a specific area of sensation; rather every particle of the body feels it.

For this reason our Lord, mighty and majestic, commanded us to perform ghusl after this act, because it occupies every particle of your constitution; and perhaps, for those who know God, one is not heedless of God, the Exalted, except in this moment; therefore the command to wash after it. This is the view of the scholars.

As for the people of gnosis of God, the people of ecstatic utterance (shath) and the people of divine outpourings, they say: God created Adam from clay and made his offspring from this living drop which He placed in Eve, and then all creation came from it after him. So there is in each of us a particle of our father Adam, for if death had befallen this particle, there would have been no offspring after Adam. This particle exists in you in the drop you discharge, from which your child comes, and it is the purest thing in you, because it is the particle that witnessed the first creation, the creation of your father Adam, peace be upon him.

We have clarified this matter before and said: If you take a centimetre of coloured material and put it in a bottle of water, then shake the bottle until the water mixes with the coloured material, each drop of the water contains a particle of this material; and likewise if you pour the bottle into a barrel, and so on.

Thus, each one of us contains a particle of our father Adam, peace be upon him. This particle witnessed the creation of Adam and witnessed the first covenant which God took from His servants in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" (172)﴾ [al-A'raf].

Therefore God, exalted is He, calls the sending of the messengers a "ba'th" (raising up), saying: ﴿God has raised up a messenger (41)﴾ [al-Furqan]: ba'thahu, as if he had been present and had an origin in a direct message from God when He took the covenant from His servants while they were in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him; as He addresses the Messenger, saying: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder (21)﴾ [al-Ghashiyah]: that is, a reminder of the old covenant which We took upon ourselves.

Therefore read the verse: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify..." (172)﴾ [al-A'raf]:

This is at the stage of the dhurr (atoms of the soul), before desire comes into souls: ﴿lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed we were unaware of this (172)," or say, "Only our fathers associated others with God before, and we were offspring after them; will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did? (173)"﴾ [al-A'raf].

Therefore: God sent the messengers to remind of the first covenant, so that heedlessness does not occur and so that the proof is established against people.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿then from a clinging clot...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: The nutfah is called 'alaqah because it clings to the womb. He, exalted is He, says in another verse: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted? (37) Then he became a clot, and He created [him] and proportioned [him] (38)﴾ [al-Qiyamah]: the mani is the fluid that carries the nutfah, which is the essence from which the foetus forms; and the 'alaqah here is the fertilised ovum. After the ovum had a clinging to the mother, and the sperm (nutfah) had a clinging to the father, they joined in a new clinging and met to cling to the wall of the womb, as if there were in them a selfhood that makes them cling to themselves; they call it the zygote.

From it comes their saying: "So-and-so is like an 'alaqah," if he is constantly with you.

After that the 'alaqah turns into a mudghah: ﴿then from a lump of flesh...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: The mudghah is a small piece of flesh the size of what is chewed of food, a mixture of several things, as if you ate, for example, a piece of meat with a spoonful of vegetables and a spoonful of rice, and by chewing it becomes a mixture; because the human body is not made of one element but of sixteen elements.

This mudghah is ﴿formed and unformed...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: the meaning of "formed" (mukhallaqah) is that the bodily frame appears on it and it takes the shape of it: this for the head, this for the arm, this for the leg, and so on; that is, it has taken the form of a human being.

As for the unformed, we have recently learned that they are the cells which replace the body and patch it when it suffers a defect; they serve as a "reserve" for re-building and repairing the tissues that have been damaged, as happens, for example, in the case of a wound: if you leave it to the body's nature, it heals gradually without leaving any trace.

We see this in the children of peasants, when one of them is wounded or some boils appear on him; they leave them to the body's natural resistance, and after a while these boils vanish without leaving any mark at all, because they have left the body to the divine pharmacy.

But if we intervene in the wound with chemical substances, or stitching or the like, it must leave a trace; you see its place shining, because these substances have damaged the body's pores; therefore such places of the body are found changed, and a person tends to scratch them, because these pores used to discharge some of the body's wastes in the form of sweat, and when these pores were blocked this phenomenon was caused. All of this is because we have interfered with the nature God created.

So the meaning of ﴿and unformed...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj] is: the divine pharmacy that replaces and rebuilds what has been damaged in the human body.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿that We may make clear to you, and We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for an appointed term...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, We clarify for you everything connected with this matter; ﴿and We cause to remain in the wombs what We will...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: this is the lump which is destined to become a foetus that completes until it is born; therefore He said: ﴿for an appointed term...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: or We cause it to fall dead before its birth.

If you say: What is the wisdom in its creation and shaping if it was destined to die as a foetus? We say: so that we know that death is an absolute matter with no tie and no age; death comes to the old man as it comes to the foetus in its mother's womb; at whatever time the term ends.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then We bring you out as a child...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: He says "nukhrijukum" (We bring you out) in the plural form, but He did not say "atfalan" (children) rather ﴿tifla(n)...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj] in the singular. Why? They say: in the language there are words in which the singular and plural are alike; so "tifl" here means "atfal" (children). "Atfal" has also occurred in another place, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty (59)﴾ [an-Nur].

Just as you say: "This is a just man" and "just men." In the story of our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, he speaks of the idols, saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me (77)﴾ [ash-Shu'ara'], and did not say "enemies." When he spoke of his guests he said: ﴿These are my guests (68)﴾ [al-Hijr], and did not say "my guests" in the plural. So the singular here carries the meaning of the plural.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿then that you may reach your maturity...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: thus the context moves us from childhood to the final stage of human life. We have previously spoken about the stages of human life: man passes through the stage of rushd (maturity): rushd of the body, when he becomes able to beget his like, and rushd of the mind, when he becomes able to act soundly and choose well between alternatives.

Then comes the stage of ashudd (full strength): ﴿until, when he reaches his full strength...(15)﴾ [al-Ahqaf]: that is, he has also matured through the events of life.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: arhal al-'umr means its worst part, when signs of feebleness and weakness appear on the person ﴿so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: because he forgets, and then he knows that his health, strength and dominion are not intrinsic to him but granted to him by God.

When a man reaches the most decrepit age he gradually returns again to the stage of childhood: he needs someone to take his hand to stand or to walk, as one takes the hand of a small child; if he speaks he stammers and falters like a child learning to talk... and so in all his affairs.

Therefore they say: early marriage is the nearest way to producing a "walid" (a parent) who will support you in the childhood of your old age; and he did not say "walad" (a child), because he will later play the part of a parent for you; they say: "laḥiqa walidahu," meaning their ages are close.

But why are some of us returned to the most decrepit age and not others? The Truthful, glorified is He, made these as examples, so that we do not say, "Would that our lives were prolonged," for if everyone's life were prolonged to the most decrepit age, the matter would become difficult for us; so it is out of God's mercy to us that He created death.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows [something] of every lovely kind (5)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, just as man was created from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then from a lump of flesh formed and unformed, then He brought him forth as a child, and he reached his full strength, and some of them died, and some are returned to the most decrepit age, so too is the state of the earth: ﴿And you see the earth barren...(5)﴾ [al-Hajj].

Hamidah: still, motionless; from it is our saying to a child who moves a great deal: "ihmad" (be still). ﴿But when We send down water upon it, it stirs...﴾

1 - Nutfah: clear water; in the Qur'an it is used for the fluid of the man or the woman from which the child is created. 'Alaqah: thick congealed blood that clings to whatever touches it. Mudghah: a piece of flesh chewed for its firmness. Mukhallaqah: a mudghah that is shaped and formed in the form of a child. Ghayr mukhallaqah: not shaped, i.e., not complete in its formation [al-Qamus al-Qawim li-l-Qur'an al-Karim].
2 - Huwa: senility and dotage to the point of not understanding. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4544].
3 - Hama' and hama'ah: black mud. Masnun: poured into a human mould or shaped into a human form, or clay like pottery suitable for shaping and polishing. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/331].
4 - Halama al-sabiyy yahlamu halaman: he reached the level of men. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/169].

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and because He gives life to the dead, and because He is over all things Competent.﴾ (6)

That is: what occurs in the creation of man, in the formation of his being, and what occurs in the sprouting and growth of crops, all of it returns to the fact that Allah, exalted is He, ﴿is the Truth.﴾ (6) [al-Hajj]. So why did He say "the Truth" and not say "the Creator"? They said: because the creator may create something and then abandon it, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Creator who is the Truth. The meaning of "the Truth" is: the Established, who does not change. Likewise His giving does not change; He, glorified is He, will continue to be the Creator who gives you every day, because His giving, glorified is He, is constant and never runs out.

If you look at the whole of existence, you will find it to be a repeating cycle. Allah, mighty and majestic, created the earth and determined its sustenance within it. For example, the quantity of water that Allah created in the universe is the very same: it has not increased nor decreased, because water has a cycle in life. The water you drink throughout your life does not diminish the amount of water that exists, because it will leave you in the form of waste to return into the water cycle of the universe anew.

So it is with the food we eat, and with the beautiful, fresh flower that we pick: everything in existence has a cycle in which it turns. This is the meaning of: ﴿and He determined in it its sustenance.﴾ (10) [Fussilat].

So the meaning of ﴿the Truth⁠﴾ (6) [al-Hajj] here is: the Established who does not change, in creation and in giving. So do not think that Allah's giving to you is something new; rather, it is an ancient giving that recurs for you and for others.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and that He gives life to the dead⁠﴾ (6) [al-Hajj]. As we said in the previous verse: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless⁠﴾ (5) [al-Hajj]: that is, still, with no life in it, and Allah alone is capable of reviving it. Therefore, the jurists call land that we prepare for cultivation "reviving the dead land" (iḥyā' al-mawāt) (1). Allah, exalted is He, alone is capable of reviving every dead thing. Therefore He says after it: ﴿and that He is over all things Competent.⁠﴾ (6) [al-Hajj].

1 – Iḥyā' al-mawāt (reviving dead land) means preparing dead land that has not previously been built up, cultivated, and made fit for benefit in dwelling, planting, and the like. For land to be considered dead (mawāt), it must be far from settlement, so that it is not a utility of it, and it is not expected to become one; reference is made to custom to determine the extent of distance from settlement. The jurists agreed that reviving is a cause of ownership, on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever revives dead land, it is his." They differed on whether the ruler's permission is required for reviving. Most scholars do not require the ruler's permission. Abu Hanifa held that the permission and approval of the Imam is required, and Malik distinguished between lands adjoining settlement and lands far from it. A just ruler may grant some individuals dead land, minerals, and waters as long as there is a public interest; if the interest is not realized, such as when the grantee does not build up or develop it, it is taken back from him. [Fiqh al-Sunna, Shaykh Sayyid Sabiq 3/201–204, adapted]

Since this is the case, and since you see with your own eyes the sign of reviving dead lands in the dead earth, do not deny the resurrection and your being brought back after death. So the Exalted says:

﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves (7)﴾:

They had already denied resurrection after death, saying:

﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? (16) Or our forefathers of old? (17)﴾ [As-Saffat]:

The Truthful, glory be to Him, responds to them: Yes, We will bring you back after death. The One who created you from nothing is certainly able to bring you back, and that is easier. Therefore He says:

﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him... (27)﴾ [Ar-Rum]: Here the Truthful, glory be to Him, addresses us according to the measure of our minds, for we understand that creating from something existing is easier than creating from nothing. As for the Creator, glorious and mighty is He, there is no easy and easier, nor light and lighter.

So His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it... (7)﴾ [Al-Hajj]: it is as if the process of reviving the dead is not the limit of Allah's power; rather, His power includes many signs and wonders. The meaning of ﴿there is no doubt about it... (7)﴾ [Al-Hajj] is: there is no suspicion in it. "The Hour" means the time of the Resurrection and its appointed moment. But the Resurrection will be for reckoning and for judging between people, so they must be raised from the graves. Therefore He says after it: ﴿And that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves (7)﴾ [Al-Hajj].

Everything that has preceded arises from the fact that He, glory be to Him, is the Truth; and because He is the Truth, He gives life to the dead, He is over all things capable, the Hour is coming with no doubt, and He will raise those who are in the graves.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And among mankind is he who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book.﴾ (8)

We spoke at the beginning of the surah about disputation by knowledge and fine exhortation, and we said: knowledge is either self-evident knowledge (ʿilm badīhī), or rational deductive knowledge (ʿilm istidlālī ʿaqlī), or knowledge through revelation from Allah, glory be to Him. As for those who dispute concerning Allah without self-evident knowledge, ﴿nor guidance…﴾ (8): meaning, rational deductive knowledge; ﴿nor an illuminating Book…﴾ (8): meaning, revelation from Allah. These are people of sophistry (safsaṭa) and barren disputation that yields no benefit. When the sensible person encounters this kind of disputation, he should not keep pace with its sophistry, for he will reach nothing beneficial with it; rather, he should move it to a sphere that does not admit sophistry.

We have in this matter an example and a model in our master Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, when he disputed with Nimrod. Read the words of Allah, exalted is He:

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, "My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west," and the one who disbelieved was overwhelmed.﴾ (258) [al-Baqarah]

Nimrod followed the method of sophistry when he said ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ (258): for he had not actually brought about death, nor actually brought about life(1). So Abraham wanted to force him into a sphere where there is no sophistry, to end this confrontation and close off to his opponent the door of obstinacy and bluster. He said ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ (258). The result was that the enemy of Allah was bewildered in his reply, ﴿and the one who disbelieved was overwhelmed﴾ (258): that is, he was astonished and perplexed.

1 - This is because Nimrod said: "I am brought two men who have deserved death, so I order one of them to be killed and he is killed, and I order the other to be pardoned and he is not killed." This was said by Qatadah, Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir (1/313). Then Ibn Kathir said: "The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he did not intend this, since it is not an answer to what Abraham said nor of its meaning, for it is a denial of the existence of the Creator; rather he intended to claim this station for himself out of obstinacy and arrogance, and to give the impression that he is the one who does that and that he is the one who gives life and causes death..."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 9:

﴿Turning aside in arrogance (thāniya ʿaṭfihi)(1) to lead [others] astray from the way of God. For him there is disgrace in this world, and We shall make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ (22:9)

﴿Thāniya ʿaṭfihi (22:9)﴾: thanā al-shay' means he twisted it, and ʿaṭf means its side. In his general makeup, a human being has a head, a neck and two shoulders, and has two sides and a back. These organs play a part in his life and movement, and indicate his conduct. So whoever argues about God without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book turns his side away from you and twists his head, because he does not like what you say. This is not because your speech is false; rather, he does not like it because he has run out of arguments and does not have the proof with which to confront you, so he has only this movement left.

For this reason, such disputation is called "mirā' " (contentious wrangling). From it comes God's words: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ (53:12), meaning: Will you argue with the Messenger of God about a matter he has seen? Mirā' is fierce argument, derived from (mariya al-ḍarʿ), meaning to milk out all the milk in it down to the last drop. The people of the countryside call this process "qarqara al-baqara," meaning that all its milk was taken and nothing remained in its udder.

Likewise, the one who argues in falsehood, or argues without knowledge or proof, you will see him being obstinate so as to take the last thing his opponent has. Had he possessed knowledge and proof, he would have ended the confrontation without quarrelling or obstinacy.

The Noble Qur'an gives us a picture of this disputation and turning away from the truth. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads away, and you see them turning aside while they are arrogant.﴾ (63:5)

The Qur'an gives us the natural gradation of turning away from the truth, which begins with turning the head, then the side, then it gives you its back and presents its shoulders. All these are signs of fleeing from argument when one is unable to persuade.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Turning aside in arrogance to lead [others] astray from the way of God...﴾ (22:9). This is the cause of turning his side: he wants to lead astray those who have been guided. Had he stood to listen to his opponent and what he presents of proofs and evidence, he would have been defeated and would not have been able to lead people astray. Therefore he turns his side, fleeing from this situation which he cannot confront or counter.

What is the reward of this type? He, exalted is He, says: ﴿For him there is disgrace in this world...﴾ (22:9). Khizy (disgrace) means humiliation and abasement. This is the reward of this world before the reward of the Hereafter. Did this disgrace not befall the disbelievers at Badr? Did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) not hold a staff in his hand before the battle and point with it, saying: "This is the place where so-and-so will fall, and this is the place where so-and-so will fall" (3), naming the chiefs of disbelief and the heads of error among Quraysh? And after the battle ended, the matter was just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had foretold, and all those chiefs fell in the very places he had pointed to.

When Abu Jahl was killed in this battle, our master ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud climbed upon him. Glory be to God! ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, the shepherd of sheep, mounted the back of the lord of Quraysh. Then Abu Jahl said, while there was still a breath of life in him: "You have climbed a difficult height, O shepherd of sheep!" meaning: "You have ridden me, O son of the [lowly] one." So what disgrace could be greater than this?

And Abu Sufyan, after al-ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him) had interceded for him with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saw the procession of the Prophet on the day of the Conquest, with the banners of the Ansar around it, a formidable and awe-inspiring procession. He could not control himself and could not hide what was in his breast, so he said to al-ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him): "The kingdom of your nephew has become mighty." He replied: "It is prophethood, O Abu Sufyan" (5), meaning: the matter is not kingship; rather it is prophethood supported by God.

And our master Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him), when people asked permission to enter upon him, gave permission to the early converts to Islam from among the slaves and freedmen, and left some of the chiefs of Quraysh at the door. Their noses swelled (fa-warrimat) with this matter and they became enraged, and among them was the father of our master Abu Bakr. He said to him: "Do you give permission to these and leave us?" He replied: "It is Islam that has placed them ahead of you." ʿUmar witnessed this scene and said to them: "What is wrong with you, your noses swollen? What is the matter with you that when they are admitted into the presence of their Lord, you hold back?"

The true anger will be in the Hereafter, when these are called to Paradise while you hold back in the terror of that station.

Recite His words: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost. Those are the ones brought near.﴾ (56:10-11)

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿We shall make them taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (22:9). This disgrace they saw in this world will not spare them from disgrace and punishment in the Hereafter. The meaning of ﴿ʿadhāb al-ḥarīq﴾ (the punishment of the Blaze): al-ḥarīq is that which burns others by its intensity, like the fire they kindled for Abraham (peace be upon him), which would roast any bird passing over it in the sky, so that it would fall roasted (7).

1 - al-ʿAṭf: the side. ʿAṭfā a person: his two sides. It is said: thanā ʿaṭfahu, meaning he turned away and withdrew his side. His words ﴿thāniya ʿaṭfihi﴾ (22:9) are a metaphor for turning away out of arrogance and conceit. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 2/25].
2 - al-Mariy: wiping the udder of a she-camel to make it yield milk. A mariy she-camel is one abundant in milk. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root m-r-y].
3 - Related by Muslim in his Sahih (1779) from the hadith of Anas (may God be pleased with him), and by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/258, 219), that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is the place where so-and-so will fall," placing his hand on the ground here and here. He said: "None of them moved from the place of the Messenger of God's hand."
4 - ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: "I found him at his last breath, so I recognized him, and I placed my foot on his neck. Abu Jahl said to him: 'You have climbed a difficult height, O shepherd of sheep.' Then I cut off his head and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I said: 'O Messenger of God, this is the head of the enemy of God, Abu Jahl.'" Related by Ibn Hisham in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (2/636).
5 - Mentioned by Ibn Hisham in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (4/404): "Abu Sufyan said: 'Glory be to God, O ʿAbbas, who are these?' I said: 'This is the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the Muhajirun and the Ansar.' He said: 'No one has the power or strength to face these.' Then he said: 'By God, O Abu al-Fadl, the kingdom of your nephew has become mighty this morning.' I said: 'O Abu Sufyan, it is prophethood.' He said: 'Then so be it.'"
6 - Warrama anfuhu means he became angry; he was swollen and puffed up with anger, and the nose is singled out because it is the seat of pride and arrogance. Warrama fulan bi-anfihi tawrīman means he lifted his nose high and acted arrogantly. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root w-r-m].
7 - Ibn Ishaq said: They gathered firewood for a month, then kindled it, and it blazed and intensified, so that a bird passing by its sides would be burned by the intensity of its heat. [Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4481)].

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿That is for what your hands have sent before, and that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ (22:10):

﴿That..﴾ (22:10) [al-Hajj]: That is, the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Blaze in the Hereafter, for what your hands have sent forward and what they have committed, not by any injustice from Us nor any transgression. Rather, you are the one who wronged yourself, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (16:118) [an-Nahl].

Did We seize them without warning, and without making this act a crime? Because you do not punish a person for a sin unless you have alerted him to it and informed him of its punishment. If you punish him without his knowing that this is a sin and that this is a crime, then you have wronged him. Therefore, the people of law say: there is no punishment except through criminalization, and no criminalization except through a text.

The text that clarifies for you and criminalizes this act has indeed come to you, and the Messengers have conveyed it to you, and the warning has preceded you, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger.﴾ (17:15) [al-Isra'].

﴿That is for what your hands have sent before..﴾ (22:10) [al-Hajj]: Is it that all sins are only the sending forth of the hand?

The sins are either sayings, or actions, or acts of the heart, such as spite or hypocrisy, for example, etc. But most sins are not committed by the hands (1).

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ (22:10) [al-Hajj]: "Ẓallām" is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha) of injustice (ẓulm). You say ẓālim (unjust). If you want intensity, you say ẓallām, just as you say: "So-and-so is ākil (eater) and so-and-so is akūl (a great eater)." The act is one, but what results from it differs. Intensity in an act may be in the act itself or in its repetition. For example, you may eat one loaf in a single meal, or you may eat five loaves in a single meal; this is intensity within one meal, though you eat three meals. Or the intensity may be in the number of meals: you eat one loaf per meal, but you eat five meals instead of three. This is intensity through repetition of the event.

The intensive form has a meaning in affirmation and a meaning in negation. If you say: "So-and-so is akūl" and affirm the intensity for him, you have affirmed the root act for him a fortiori, so he is ākil. If you negate the intensity, the negation of the intensity does not negate the root. You say: "So-and-so is not akūl," and this does not negate that he is ākil.

If we apply this rule to His saying: ﴿And that Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ (22:10) [al-Hajj]: this would mean that He, glorified and exalted is He, is "unjust" (ẓālim), far be it from Allah. Here we say: there are other verses that negate the act, such as His saying: ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone.﴾ (18:49) [al-Kahf], and His saying: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were themselves the wrongdoers.﴾ (43:76) [az-Zukhruf].

Moreover, the intensive form here is attached to "the servants," so if we assume intensity, it is intensity through repetition of the event: ﴿ẓallām lil-'abīd﴾ (22:10): He wrongs this one, wrongs that one, and wrongs that one, and the wronged are servants, not a single servant.

Injustice in its reality is that the strong takes the right of the weak, and the injustice is in proportion to the strength and capacity of the unjust. Accordingly, if injustice were to come from Allah, exalted is He, in proportion to His might and power, it would undoubtedly be a severe injustice that no one could bear. So we do not say "unjust" (ẓālim) but "ẓallām," and thus the meaning accords with the intensive form.

So the Truth, glorified is He, is not ẓallām to the servants, because He has distinguished between the lawful and the unlawful, between the crime and has set for it a punishment, and the Messengers have conveyed from the very beginning, so there is no proof for anyone.

1 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4548): "He expressed the whole by the hand, because the hand is what acts and seizes for the whole.."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 22, verse 11:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge. If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial afflicts him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the clear loss.﴾ (22:11)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge…﴾ (22:11). Worship ('ibadah) means that you obey Allah in what He commands, carrying it out, and obey Him in what He forbids, abstaining from it. Some people worship Allah in this manner for as long as they are in constant good and continuous joy. But when harm strikes them or something disliked befalls them, they turn back on their faces: ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial afflicts him, he turns back on his face.﴾ (22:11)

Allah, glorified is He, wants His servant to come to His worship with a steadfast faith, one that the events of life do not shake and that does not waver and retreat. Your Lord wants you to be His servant in good and in evil, in ease and in hardship, for both are a trial and a test. You did not believe in Allah except because you knew that He is a wise, just, and capable God, and you must take whatever events of life befall you in the light of these attributes.

If life weighs heavily on you, know that behind this there is wisdom. If it is not for you, then it is for your children after you. For perhaps, when they find you in abundance and good, they will become covetous, corrupt, and transgressive. And perhaps a life of constraint, scarce provision, and your toil to secure for them the necessities of life will be a motive for them.

Read His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ (96:6–7), and His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial; and to Us you will be returned.﴾ (21:35).

You must know these realities and believe in the wisdom of your Lord in all that He brings upon you, whether it be bounty or misery. If sickness confines you to your house, then say: What has happened outside the house? May God keep me far from it and grant me well-being from it? For perhaps the good lies in what you consider evil, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you.﴾ (2:216).

Statisticians have conducted surveys on some of our homes and found brothers in one household, under one set of environmental conditions, with one father and one mother, and even with the same level of schooling at school. Yet you find one of the children upright and committed, and the other at the opposite extreme. When they researched the cause of this phenomenon, they found that the upright son's period of upbringing and childhood coincided with a time when his father was ill and confined to his home for six years. So this son received the greatest share of care and upbringing, and did not get the opportunity to go out of the house or mix with bad companions.

In another case of a delinquent son, they found that the cause of his deviation was that his father, during the period of his upbringing and training, was a merchant who travelled often, yet he would lavish on his family. So the boy was raised in ease of living, without the father's supervision.

In yet another case they found two brothers, one outstanding and the other a failure. When they investigated the reasons, despite their living under the same conditions, they found that the outstanding son had weak health, so he inclined to home, reading, and study, while the other was healthy and handsome, so he inclined to a life of luxury and spent most of his time outside the house. Examples in this field are many.

So trials have their gains, and behind them are wisdoms, for they arise and flow over you by the wisdom of your Lord and Creator, and they are not from your striving nor from the work of your hands. Since this is so, be content with them, and worship Allah with sincerity and steadfast faith in good and in evil.

As for the meaning of ﴿worships Allah on an edge…﴾ (22:11): the harf (edge) is the extremity of a thing. It is like when you enter and find the room full, so you sit on the edge at the end of those seated. This is usually not accompanied by settledness and tranquility. Likewise, one who worships Allah "on an edge" means that faith has not settled in his heart, and a trial soon drives him out of faith, because he worshipped Allah with a worship that is not firmly rooted in the certainty that issues from a believer in a wise God regarding what He brings upon His servant.

The verse has left out none of the preoccupations of the human soul, whether in good or in evil.

Consider the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿If good befalls him…﴾ (22:11), and likewise: ﴿…and if a trial afflicts him…﴾ (22:11). You do not say "I attained good"; rather, good is what reached you and came to your door. You do not seek your provision as much as it seeks you. Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and provide for him from where he does not expect.﴾ (65:2–3).

People of knowledge say: Your provision knows your location better than you know its location; that is, it knows your address, but you do not know its address. The proof is that you may seek provision in a place and receive nothing from it, while you may see the crops in the fields flourishing, hoping for an abundant harvest and building your hopes upon them, and then a storm or a blight comes upon them, and you receive nothing from them, not even enough to quench your thirst.

There is a lesson and an example in Ibn Udhaynah when his circumstances became straitened in Medina. They said to him: You have a companionship with Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad caliph, so go to him and you will obtain some good from the caliphate. Indeed Ibn Udhaynah travelled to his friend, driving the livers of camels until he reached Syria. He asked permission and was granted it, and his companion received him and asked about his condition. He said: "I am in constraint and hardship." Now in the caliph's assembly there were scholars, and he said to him: "O Urwah, are you not the one who said — and Ibn Udhaynah was a poet:

*'I have known, and extravagance is not my nature, that what is my provision will come to me.'*"

At this, Urwah felt that the caliph had broken his heart and disappointed his hope in him, so he said: "May Allah reward you with good, O Commander of the Faithful. You have reminded me of what I had forgotten, and alerted me to what I had neglected," and then he departed.

When Ibn Udhaynah left the caliph's assembly, the caliph reflected on the situation and reproached himself for his conduct toward his companion, whose good he had sought, and how he had sent him away in this manner. So he wished to correct this error and sent a messenger carrying many gifts. But every time the caliph's messenger followed Ibn Udhaynah to one place, he found that he had left for another, until he reached his house, knocked on the door, and informed him that the Commander of the Faithful regretted what had happened, and these were his gifts and presents.

At this, Ibn Udhaynah completed his first verse, saying:

*'I strive for it, and its seeking wearies me; but had I sat, it would come to me without my concern.'*

Likewise we notice in this verse: ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial afflicts him…﴾ (22:11), that it did not set good against evil, but called it "a trial" (fitnah), meaning a test and an affliction, because he may succeed in this test, and then it will not be evil for him.

As for the meaning of ﴿he turns back on his face﴾ (22:11): it means the matter is reversed. After having been a worshipper and obedient, he turns to the opposite and becomes disobedient. ﴿He has lost this world and the Hereafter﴾ (22:11): the loss of a person's worship is a great loss that cannot be compensated nor replaced by anything. Therefore He says after it: ﴿That is the clear loss﴾ (22:11). So is there a clear loss and a loss that is not clear?

Yes: loss is a loss that can be compensated; but a loss for which there is no compensation is the clear loss, which accompanies a person and does not leave him. It is a loss not confined to this world alone, which one may compensate for or endure with patience, but extends to the Hereafter, where there is no compensation for its loss and no patience for its severity. Thus "clear loss" means the all-encompassing loss that encircles its possessor.

Therefore we say to one who has lost someone dear to him, such as a woman who has lost her only son: If the deceased was beloved and precious, then sell him dearly and enter Paradise with him. That is when you are patient over his loss and seek his reward from Allah. But if you have lost the world through him, do not lose the Hereafter through him. For if we slap our cheeks, tear our garments, and object to the decree of Allah concerning him, then we have lost through him both this world and the Hereafter.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke truly when he said: "How wondrous is the affair of the believer, for all of his affairs are good. If ease befalls him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if hardship befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him. And this is only for the believer."

Patience at trial and gratitude in ease is one of the levels of faith and a stage of certainty in the soul of the believer. It is a beginning and a threshold, followed by other stages and ascents, according to the strength of faith.

Listen to this dialogue that took place between the people of knowledge among the ascetics, and how they vied to attain these stations of faith and competed in them, not out of vanity and boasting, but out of sincere intention to ascend in faith.

One of these accomplished ones asked his companion: "How are the ascetics in your land?" He said: "If good befalls us, we give thanks, and if evil befalls us, we are patient." The shaykh laughed and said: "And what is so special about that? That is the condition of dogs in Balkh. As for us: if good befalls us, we prefer others, and if evil befalls us, we give thanks."

This is not boasting but rivalry. Both men are ascetics traversing the path of Allah, each considering himself counted among this path, and so each strives to ascend to its highest levels. So beware of thinking that the goal is patience at trial and gratitude for bounty; that is the beginning, and after it are higher stations and loftier ascents for whoever seeks eminence and girds up the sleeve of earnestness in worshipping his Lord.

Look at one of these ascetics saying to his companion: "Do you not long for Allah?" He said: "No." He said, astonished: "And how is that?" He said: "One longs only for one who is absent, and when has He been absent from me so that I should long for Him?" Thus are the degrees of faith and the transparency of the relationship between the servant and his Lord, mighty and majestic is He.

1 – Occasion of revelation: several narrations have been reported regarding it, among them:
- From Ibn Abbas, who said: Some of the Bedouins used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ), embrace Islam, and then return to their lands. If they found a year of rain, a year of fertility, and a year of good birth, they would say: "Indeed this religion of ours is good, so hold fast to it." But if they found a year of drought, a year of bad birth, and a year of famine, they would say: "There is no good in this religion of ours." So Allah revealed to His Prophet: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it…﴾ (22:11). Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/209), and al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 175).
- From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: A Jewish man embraced Islam, then he lost his sight, his wealth, and his children, and he considered Islam ill-omened. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Release me from it." He said: "Islam does not admit of release." He said: "I have found no good in my religion; it took away my sight, my wealth, and my children." He said: "O Jew, Islam purifies men as fire purifies the dross of iron, silver, and gold." He said: And there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge…﴾ (22:11).
2 – He is Urwah ibn Yahya (whose laqab is Udhaynah) ibn Malik ibn al-Harith al-Laythi: an eminent poet of love poetry, from the people of Medina; he is also counted among the jurists and transmitters of hadith, but poetry predominates in him. He died around 130 AH [al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 4/227].
3 – Al-Zirikli cited this verse and the one following it in his book al-A'lam (4/227) from the poetry of Urwah ibn Udhaynah. See also: al-Shi'r wa'l-shu'ara' 225; Fawat al-wafayat 2/34.
4 – Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (2299), Kitab al-Zuhd, and by Ahmad in his Musnad (5/24), and al-Darimi in his Sunan (2/318), from the hadith of Suhayb al-Rumi, may Allah be pleased with him.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says about this one who worships Allah "on an edge":

﴿He calls, besides Allah, upon that which neither harms him nor benefits him. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ (12)

The meaning of ﴿what neither harms him...﴾ (12) [al-Hajj]: Can the idol that the disbeliever worships besides Allah harm him? No. The idol does not harm.
