Rather, what truly harms is the one who opposes Him and turns away from His worship: the Lordship he opposes harms him, and the Recompenser who repays him for his deeds harms him. So what is the meaning of ﴿harms him...﴾ (12) [al-Hajj] here?

The meaning: it does not harm him if he turns away from it and does not worship it, and it does not benefit him if he worships it. ﴿That is the far-reaching error﴾ (12) [al-Hajj]: Yes, it is error, because a person worships and obeys whoever he hopes will benefit him in anything, or whom he fears may harm him in anything.

We have mentioned earlier the saying of some of the knowers ('arifin): "Make your obedience to One whom you need not be independent of." If we were to teach this saying to our children in their school books, and those responsible for upbringing gave it attention, it would not have led children to seduce one another into corruption. A child would stop and think once and a thousand times about the guidance of his Lord and the advice of his father and mother, and how he would abandon the guidance of those who love him, fear for him and wish him good, in favour of the enticement of a friend about whom he knows nothing of his character.

We must feed our children the principles of Islam, so that the child knows from his youth who loves him and who hates him, and who is more deserving of his obedience.

You notice in the verse that harm precedes benefit: ﴿what neither harms him nor benefits him...﴾ (12) [al-Hajj]. This is because warding off corruption (dar' al-mafsadah) takes precedence over securing benefit (jalb al-maslahah). Corruption is the departure of a thing from the soundness of its creation, whereas benefit adds to you and increases you, while harm diminishes you. Therefore it is better for you to remain as you are, neither diminished nor increased. So when you stand before two matters, one bringing good and the other repelling evil, there is no doubt that you will choose to repel evil first, and occupy yourself with warding off corruption before securing benefit.

We gave an example for this: suppose a person is about to throw you an apple, and another is about to throw a stone at you at the same time. What do you do? Do you take the apple, or guard against the harm of the stone? This is the meaning of "warding off corruption takes precedence over securing benefit."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 22, verse 13:

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Surely wretched is the patron, and surely wretched is the companion.﴾

The preceding verse establishes that he calls upon what neither harms him nor benefits him, and this verse establishes that he calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit.

The form of the comparative (ʾafʿal al-tafḍīl), here "nearer" (aqrab), indicates that two things share a single attribute, but one of them exceeds the other in that attribute. If you say, "So-and-so is better than so-and-so," this means that both are good, but one exceeds the other in goodness.

So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit...﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 13] means: there is a benefit, and it is near, but harm is nearer than it. In its outward meaning this verse seems to contradict the preceding verse. In truth there is no contradiction, and this matter must be understood in light of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 82].

The idols they worshipped had custodians (sadana, sing. sadin) who exercised control over them and over their worshippers. When they wanted something from the deities, they would say to the custodians: "Call upon the gods for us for such-and-such." Thus they had influence and temporal authority, and they were the intermediaries between the idols and their worshippers. This intermediary role brought them much good and gave them many benefits, so they would take everything that was offered to the idols.

So the idols are, in this sense, a cause of benefit to their custodians, but this benefit at most lasts in this world, and then they leave it at death. The period of benefit is short, and perhaps death reaches him before he profits from what he has taken. And if death comes, there is no faith, no deed, and no repentance. This is the meaning of ﴿whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 13].

Therefore, after it, He says: ﴿Surely wretched is the patron, and surely wretched is the companion﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 13]. The word (biʾsa, "wretched") is said in blame, and it means: evil and ugly. The mawlā (patron) is the one who is close to you and near you, and what is meant by him is the one who benefits you, because you draw near only to the one who benefits you: either because he helps you at the time of hardship, supports you in distress, and aids you when you need his support—and this is the walī (protector)—or because you bring him close to you since he consoles you, keeps you company, and you find comfort in him, but he is weak and cannot support you—and this is the ʿashīr (companion).

The idols they worshipped are the wretched patron, because they do not aid them at the time of hardship, and the wretched companion, because they do not console them, and they do not find comfort in them outside of times of hardship.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 14:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills.﴾ (14)

After the Truth, may He be glorified and exalted, spoke of the disbelievers, the people of the Fire, and those who worship Allah "on an edge" (ḥarf), it was necessary that He bring the counterpart, because the soul is disposed to comparison and reflection on the causes of entering the Fire and the causes of entering Paradise, and this is more effective in establishing the proof.

Among the same is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss. And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.﴾ [al-Infitar: 13-14], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let them laugh a little and weep much...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 82].

Mentioning the blessing alone, without its opposite, the punishment, does not produce the desired effect; but when blessing is set against punishment, and the removal of harm is set against the granting of benefit, each of them reveals the other. Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has certainly succeeded...﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185]. For if you believe, you are not merely drawn away from the Fire, although that in itself is a blessing; rather, you are drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise.

Faith (al-iman) is an act of the heart and inner states by which the soul is at rest. But faith has a requirement: you believed in Allah, and your heart was reassured that Allah is the Creator, the Provider, the Necessary Existent, and so on. So what is the requirement of this faith?

The requirement of faith is that you listen to His commands, because He is the All-Wise; that you trust in His power, because He is the All-Powerful; that you fear His seizure, because He is the Compeller (al-Jabbar); that you do not despair of His expansion, because He is the Expander (al-Basit); and that you do not feel safe from His restriction, because He is the Restrainer (al-Qabid).

You have believed in all these matters. So when He commands you with a command, you must bring to mind the grounds of this command, while being certain that your Lord, mighty and majestic, did not command you or forbid you from emptiness, but rather through the attributes of perfection in Him, glory be to Him, or the attributes of majesty and dominance. So bring these attributes to mind in all your deeds and in everything you do or refrain from.

Therefore, the verse combined faith and righteous deeds: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens...﴾ (14) [al-Hajj].

And in Surah al-'Asr: ﴿By time. Indeed, mankind is in loss. Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds...﴾ (1-3) [al-'Asr]. Not only that, but also: ﴿and advise each other to truth and advise each other to patience﴾ (3) [al-'Asr].

So mutual advice toward truth and steadfastness in the face of hardships is a response to the call of faith and one of its fruits, because the believer, in the journey of life, will be exposed to many trials that may shake him, will face mockery and ridicule, and may be subjected to various kinds of torment.

So he must, therefore, hold fast to the truth and advise his brother to it, and he must be patient and advise his brothers to patience. This is because a person may be exposed to periods of weakness and faltering, so the strong, at a time of trial, must counsel the weak.

Perhaps this situation changes in another position and before another trial: the one you advise today to be patient may advise you tomorrow, and thus mutual advice toward truth and mutual advice toward patience bears fruit in the community of faith.

So: advise one another, for you will be exposed to shocks, not all-encompassing shocks, but shocks that some face and others do not. If you weaken, you will find among your brothers one who consoles you: be patient, be steadfast, seek reward. Beware lest trial dislodge you from the truth, or lead you out of patience. These are the elements of salvation that believers must hold fast to: faith, righteous deeds, mutual advice toward truth, and mutual advice toward patience.

As for His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow...﴾ (14) [al-Hajj]: al-Jannat (the gardens) are the orchards and groves full of kinds of delights: crops, greenery, freshness, flowers, and pleasant fragrance, all of which are the product of water. Therefore He said: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ (14) [al-Hajj]. The meaning of ﴿from beneath them﴾ (14) [al-Hajj] is that the water is inherent in them, not coming to them from another place that might be cut off from them, as in another verse: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ (100) [al-Tawbah].

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾ (14) [al-Hajj], because nothing overpowers Him, and He does not deal with His acts as humans deal with theirs. ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (82) [Ya-Sin]. If you reflect on this verse, you will find that the thing Allah wills and commands to exist is in reality existent, as evidenced by the fact that Allah addresses it: ﴿He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (82) [Ya-Sin]. So it is, therefore, actually existent and real, and the command here is only for its manifestation in the world of observation.

1 - I.e., He rewards whom He wills and punishes whom He wills; for the believers is Paradise by virtue of His true promise and His grace, and for the disbelievers is the Fire by virtue of His justice that preceded. [Said by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (6/4552)].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 15:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not give him victory in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch out a rope to the sky and then cut it off, and then see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him.﴾ (15)

(Yazunnu) conveys knowledge that is not certain and not confirmed. We have already discussed the attribution of propositions (nisbat al-qadaya). There is a judgement made and a subject about which it is made. You say: "Zayd is diligent (mujtahid)." You believe that diligence is attributed to Zayd. If your belief is correct, you can present the evidence for its correctness, saying: "The proof is that he passes every year with distinction."

But if he holds this proposition without offering evidence for it, as when he hears people say "Zayd is diligent" and repeats what they say, while he has no proof for the truth of this statement, it is like the child whom we teach: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (1) [al-Ikhlas]. This proposition is factual and the child believes it, but he cannot present evidence for it until he grows up and his thinking matures.

So from where did the child take this proposition and believe it? He took it on the authority of the one he trusts: his father or his teacher, and then he imitated him. Thus: if the proposition is true but you cannot establish evidence for it, it is taqlid (imitation). If you believe a true proposition and establish evidence for it, this is the highest level of knowledge. If you believe a proposition that is not true, this is ignorance (jahl).

The ignorant person is one who believes something that is not true, and this is what wearies the whole world and makes those around him miserable. The ignorant person who knows nothing and has no idea he believes in is a blank slate: you can persuade him of the truth and he will accept it from you, because his mind is empty and he does not oppose you.

As for the ignorant person who holds a mistaken idea, he first needs you to convince him of the error of his idea so that he gives it up, and then you can present to him the correct idea.

If you are in doubt about the attribution, such that the attribution of error and the attribution of correctness are equal for you, this is shakk (doubt). You cannot affirm Zayd's diligence, nor deny it. If the likelihood of diligence predominates, it is zann (supposition); if the likelihood of non-diligence predominates, it is wahm (illusion).

Thus, the attribution of propositions is one of the following: 'ilm (knowledge) which you believe, which is true, and for which you can establish evidence; or taqlid (imitation), which is what you believe that is true but cannot establish evidence for; or jahl (ignorance), when you believe something untrue; or shakk (doubt), when you do not affirm a thing and affirmation and negation are equal for you; or zann (supposition), when you favour affirmation; or wahm (illusion), when you favour negation.

So zann in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not give him victory...﴾ (15) [al-Hajj] means: there passes through his mind, merely in passing, that Allah will not give Muhammad victory, or he imagines this, and only the disbelievers imagine this, because they hope for it in the battle between faith and disbelief. Whoever holds this supposition must give it up, because it is a remote matter that will not happen and will not occur.

The disbelievers held this supposition when they saw the first signs of the victory of faith and the tokens of its triumph, and they were enraged by this, and they found nothing to ease their hearts except this supposition.

Therefore, God returns their rage upon them, saying to them: You will remain in your rage, because victory belongs to faith and its soldiers continuously. There is nothing for you but to make a rope in the sky and tie your neck to it, hanging yourself until you fall. If this scheme against yourself will save you from rage, then do it: ﴿let him stretch out a rope to the sky and then cut it off, and then see whether his scheming removes that which enrages him﴾ (15) [al-Hajj].

But what is ghayz (rage)? Ghayz is a kind of anger mixed with sorrow, grief and regret, when you see a reality happening before your eyes that does not please you, and at the same time you cannot do anything to prevent what displeases you.

This root (gh-y-z) occurs in other places in the Book of Allah, and it has been used even of inanimate things that do not feel. Read the words of Allah, exalted is He, about the Fire: ﴿It nearly bursts with rage﴾ (8) [al-Mulk], and He said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ (12) [al-Furqan]. It is as if the Fire is enraged at these people, preparing itself for them and awaiting them.

Rage happens to both the believer and the disbeliever. When we see the obstinacy of the disbelievers and their mockery and ridicule of faith, we are enraged, but Allah removes the rage from our hearts, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿and removes the rage of their hearts﴾ (15) [al-Tawbah].

As for the disbelievers' rage at the victory of faith, it will remain in their hearts. Our Lord, glory be to Him, says to them: Be completely certain that Allah has never sent a messenger without guaranteeing that He will support him. If any other thought crosses your minds, it will not relieve you or heal your rage unless you hang yourselves. Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, addressed them in another verse, saying: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ (119) [Al 'Imran].

As for the meaning of ﴿let him stretch out a rope to the sky﴾ (15) [al-Hajj] and ﴿let him stretch out﴾ (15): from madda al-shay' (to stretch a thing), meaning: to lengthen it after it was gathered together. From it is His saying: ﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾ (19) [al-Hijr]. So wherever you walk, you find an earth extended, with no end and no edge.

The sabab (means) is the rope, with which they draw water from the well. But can anyone tie a rope to the sky? Thus He has made the matter depend on something impossible, as if He is saying to them: Even if you want to hang yourselves, you will not be able to, and you will remain in your rage.

Or the meaning may be: ﴿to the sky﴾ (15): i.e., the sky of the house and its ceiling, like someone who hangs himself from the ceiling of a house.

And one may understand sabab as anything that brings you to the sky, and any means of ascent. The meaning would then be: take any way that will bring you to the sky in order to prevent Muhammad from the causes of victory, because the victory of Muhammad comes from the sky, so block it. This too they cannot do, and their rage will remain in their hearts.

You will notice that we are speaking of Muhammad (ﷺ), although the verse does not mention him. All that appears in the verse is the third-person singular pronoun in His words: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not give him victory...﴾ (15) [al-Hajj]. The discourse is directed at the disbelievers enraged by the first signs of victory for the company of faith. So His words ﴿give him victory﴾ (15) — whom does He give victory to? It must be Muhammad. Why?

They said: Because names, when they are uttered, indicate meanings. When you say "sky" we understand what is meant; when you say "heart" we understand; "light" we know what is meant. Names are either apparent nouns, such as Muhammad, 'Ali, 'Umar, earth and sky, or pronouns which refer to these apparent nouns, such as: I, you, he, they. The pronoun is ambiguous and is specified only by the context: you say "I", and others say "I" or "we", so what specifies the speaking pronoun is the situation of address. The essence of understanding in pronouns is the speaker and the addressee. If one is neither speaker nor addressee, he is absent. So from where does the indication of definiteness for the absent come?

When you say "he", "she", "they", which is meant by these pronouns? How do you specify them? If you specify the speaker by his speech and the addressee by being addressed, how do you specify the absent? They said: There must be something preceding it that indicates it, as when you say: "A man came to me and I honoured him": whom did you honour? You honoured the man you were speaking of. "A woman came to me and I honoured her." "A group came, so-and-so, and I honoured them." Thus the referent of the pronoun is that which indicates it.

But no mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has preceded the pronoun to specify and indicate him. Yes, there has been no prior mention of the Messenger of Allah, but reflect on the meaning: the discourse here concerns victory between the company of faith, headed by Muhammad (ﷺ), and the company of disbelief, headed by these obstinate people. So the context necessarily determines that the pronoun refers only to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

An example of this is His words: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it﴾ (1) [al-Qadr]: the pronoun here is determined and refers only to the Qur'an. The pronoun is determined only when the mind does not turn to anything else in its context.

Read: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (1) [al-Ikhlas]. You notice that the pronoun precedes the apparent noun, so the referent comes later, yet the pronoun refers only to Allah. When it is said "He" alone in this way, it can refer only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Likewise in His words: ﴿And if Allah were to punish people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] any creature﴾ (61) [al-Nahl]: upon the back of what? In this context the mind turns only to the earth.

And His words: ﴿then let him look, does his scheming remove that which enrages him?﴾ (15) [al-Hajj]: the interrogation here is from one who knows; it is an interrogation for affirmation, so that they themselves may acknowledge that their rage will remain as it is, that nothing will cure it, and that they will die in their rage, as He said: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ (119) [Al 'Imran].

1 - Two interpretations of this verse have been reported:
1- Whoever thinks that Allah will not give victory to Muhammad (ﷺ) in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch out a rope — i.e., to the sky, the sky of his house — then let him cut it off, i.e., let him strangle himself with it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Qatadah and others.
2- Whoever thinks that Allah will not give victory to His Prophet and that this matter will be cut off from him, let him cut it off at its root, from the direction from which it comes, for its root is in the sky. ("Then let him cut off") i.e., from the Prophet, the revelation that comes to him from Allah, if he is able. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.
Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/210): "The statement of Ibn 'Abbas and his companions is more preferable and more evident in meaning and more forceful in mockery." See al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti (6/15, 16). Shaykh al-Sha'rawi, may Allah have mercy on him, held both opinions, for both are sound and possible, and Allah knows best.
2 - This root occurs in the Noble Qur'an:
- yughiz (the verb in the present tense): occurs 3 times (al-Tawbah 12) (al-Hajj 15) (al-Fath 29).
- al-ghayz (the noun with the definite article): occurs 4 times (Al 'Imran 119-134) (al-Tawbah 15) (al-Mulk 8).
- bi-ghaydikum (the noun preceded by the prepositional letter ba' and annexed to the second-person plural pronoun): occurs once (al-Ahzab 25).
- la-ghaythun (the active participle, plural, emphasised with lam): occurs once (al-Shu'ara' 55).
- taghayyuzan (the verbal noun of tagayyaza): occurs once (al-Furqan 12).
3 - al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4553): "The pronoun in ﴿Allah will give him victory﴾ (15) [al-Hajj] refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). Although he has not been mentioned, the whole discourse indicates him, because faith is faith in Allah and in Muhammad, and turning away from the religion is turning away from the religion that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And thus We have sent it down as clear verses, and that Allah guides whom He wills.﴾ (16)

His saying: "We have sent it down" (16): i.e., the Qur'an, because the pronoun here, as we have mentioned, has a definite referent, and as long as its referent is definite it does not need a prior mention. Sending down (inzal) carries the meaning of height. So if you find in this legislation that has come to you in the Qur'an something that is hard for you or that stands between you and what your soul desires, know that it comes from one above you, from Allah, and not from an equal to you whom you could correct or debate, asking: "Why this command? Why this prohibition?" As long as the command comes to you from Allah, you must hear and obey, and not argue.

We have an example in this submission in our master Abu Bakr when they said to him: "Your companion claims that he was taken by night from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis, and then ascended with him to the heaven." The Siddiq replied only: "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth,"(1) just like that, without debate, for the command is from above, from Allah.

We have also said: If you visited a sick man and found many medicines beside him, and you asked him: "Why all this medicine?" he said: "The doctor prescribed it," and you began to object to this medicine, mentioning its interactions, its harms and its ingredients, and you inserted yourself into a matter that is none of your business.

This is an analogy with a difference, and with acknowledgment of the errors of physicians in prescribing medicine, but to clarify the matter, and to God belongs the highest likeness. The poet said truly:

Glory be to Him who inherits the physician and his medicine, and shows the patient the deaths of the cautious.

So: the proof for any command is not that we know its wisdom; it suffices that we know the one who commands it.

The meaning of ﴿verses﴾ (16): i.e., wonders. ﴿Clear﴾ (16): i.e., evident. We have previously mentioned that the word "verses" (āyāt) is applied to three meanings: the cosmic signs that establish God's power, through which faith settles in souls, such as the night and the day, the sun and the moon; the verses in the sense of miracles accompanying the messengers to establish the truthfulness of their message from God; and the verses of which the Qur'an is composed, called "bearers of rulings" (ḥāmilat al-aḥkām).

So the meaning here, ﴿And thus We have sent it down as clear verses﴾ (16), is that the word "verses" carries all these meanings: the verses of the Qur'an include the cosmic signs, include the miracle, and are themselves the verses of rulings.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿and that Allah guides whom He wills﴾ (16). This is among the matters over which people have stood at length: ﴿He misleads whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ (93, al-Nahl), and similar verses, which those who have no share of guidance hold on to. They say: "Allah has not willed guidance for us, so what can we do? What is our fault?"

This is a mistaken intellectual stance, for the intellectual stance requires that you mention a thing and its counterpart. But these people have alerted the mind to the contradiction in one [verse] and left the other, so it is, therefore, a justificatory stance. The one who is astray says: "Allah has decreed misguidance for me, so what is my fault? Why did He not say: 'the obedient one, for whom Allah decreed guidance, why does He reward him?'"

So why do you leave the good and argue about the evil?

Whoever reflects on the verses that speak of Allah's will regarding misguidance and guidance finds that He, glorified is He, has explained whom He wills to misguide and whom He wills to guide. Read His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ (67, al-Ma'idah), so his disbelief preceded His not guiding him; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾ (6, al-Munafiqun), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ (50, al-Qasas). He only guides the one who believes in Him. As for those who chose disbelief, were content with it and inclined to it, Allah, Exalted is He, seals their hearts, so faith does not enter them, and disbelief does not leave them, because they loved it, so He increased them in it, just as He increased the believers in faith: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ (17, Muhammad).

Guidance here means pointing to good, and we have previously given an example of it, and to God belongs the highest likeness: suppose you are taking a road you do not know, so you stop at a traffic policeman and ask him about your destination, and he directs you to it and describes for you the road that leads to it. But does his guidance oblige you to take the road he described to you?

Of course you are free to travel it or some other. If you then keep the policeman's kindness in mind and thank him for it, and he perceives good in you, he will himself help you over the obstacles of the road, and may even ride with you to pass you through a dangerous area he fears for you. This is the meaning of ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ (17, Muhammad).

But if you look down upon this man, or accuse him of not knowing the routes, he will leave you to yourself and withhold even mere advice from you.

Likewise... the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, guides the believer and guides the disbeliever to good. The believer is content with Allah and accepts His command and prohibition, and praises Allah for this blessing, so He increases him in faith and helps him bear the hardship of worship, and makes for him a light by which he walks by His guidance. As for the disbeliever, He leaves him stumbling in the darkness of his disbelief and wandering in the labyrinths of blindness and misguidance.

1 - Ibn Hisham mentioned it in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (1/398), and al-Hakim recorded it in his Mustadrak (3/62) and declared it authentic, and al-Dhahabi affirmed it, from the hadith of ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians (1), and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated [others with Allah] – indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things. (17)﴾

These are six groups, of which Allah informed by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection...(17)﴾ [al-Hajj]. The meaning of "judging between them" is that there is disagreement and conflict among them. If you follow the verses that mention these groups, you will find that there are two verses, in al-Baqarah and in al-Ma'idah.

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians and the Sabians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds – for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve (62)﴾ [al-Baqarah].

In al-Ma'idah He puts the Sabians before the Christians, and in this place He comes with the nominative case using the conjunction (waw), He says:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians – whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds – no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve (69)﴾ [al-Ma'idah].

﴿Those who believed...(17)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, in Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And those who were Jews...(17)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, the Jews. Then the Christians; and these two were before Islam. As for the Sabians: they are a group who were upon the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), then they worshipped the stars, so they were named Sabians for their departure from the true religion. As for the Magians: they are the worshippers of fire. And those who associated: they are the polytheists, worshippers of idols and images.

As for the advancement and postponement between the Christians and the Sabians, they said: because the Christians are a large, well-known sect and have a prophet; as for the Sabians, they were a group who rebelled against their prophet, opposed him, and brought a creed other than his, so they are few. However, they preceded the Christians in chronological order. Therefore, when chronological precedence is observed, He says: ﴿the Sabians and the Christians...(17)﴾ [al-Hajj], and when numbers and fame are observed, He says: ﴿the Christians and the Sabians...(62)﴾ [al-Baqarah]. So each of the advancement or the postponement is intended for a specific meaning.

As for His saying: ﴿and the Sabians...(69)﴾ [al-Ma'idah] in the nominative, against the rule of coordination, since it was coordinated to a accusative word, and the coordinated word follows the word it is coordinated to in its grammatical case, why then was a nominative word placed in the middle of accusative words?

They said: the nominative is not complete among the accusatives except after the completion of the sentence. It is as if He said: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians," and "the Sabians likewise." So here He coordinated a complete sentence; it is postponed in meaning and advanced in wording. Thus the verse includes the advancement and postponement mentioned above.

But how does disagreement arise among the religions?

Disagreement arises from the fact that a people believe in a God and believe in the prophet who conveys from this God, but they differ among themselves on matters, as we see, for example, the disagreement between the Mu'tazilah and the Ahl al-Sunnah, or the Jabriyyah and the Qadariyyah: one group affirms the attributes, and others deny them; one group says: man is compelled in his actions, and others say: rather, he is free.

Disagreement may also arise among religions due to differences concerning prophethood. The adherents of the religions believe in the Acting, Choosing God, but they differ regarding the prophets Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad, although they are all true. Disagreement may also arise from false claims, like those who claim prophethood, such as those who worship fire, or who worship Buddha, for example.

So these are six different groups which the verse mentions. What is the ruling on all of them after the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ)?

We say: as for the polytheists who worshipped idols, and likewise those who worshipped a claimed prophethood, these are lost disbelievers. As for the Jews and Christians who believe in an Acting, Choosing God and believe in a true prophethood, their situation after the rise of Islam is that Allah, the Exalted, has established for us a final purification of these religions. Whoever was a Jew before Islam, or a Christian before Islam, Allah has made for them a doctrinal purification within Islam; so if they were believers in the first faith in Allah, the Exalted, they must begin anew as believing Muslims.

Therefore He said after it: ﴿whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds – for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve (62)﴾ [al-Baqarah].

So after the rise of Islam, a new life began for all of these – the Jews, the Christians, the Magians and the polytheists – and a new page was opened for them in which they are "children of today," since faith in Allah, the Exalted, and faith in His prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) became binding upon them all, as if Islam is a faith-based clearance sale (and "Okazion") that wipes out what preceded it, and "Allah has pardoned what is past."

When the Truth, glorified is He, spoke of the generations preceding the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), He said: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said, "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on this condition?" They said, "We affirm it." He said, "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses." (81)﴾ [Al 'Imran].

Therefore both Musa and 'Isa (peace be upon them both) alerted to the existence of Muhammad (ﷺ) and gave glad tidings of him, as evidenced by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it... (89)﴾ [al-Baqarah]: and what is meant is the Jews and Christians.

Muhammad (ﷺ) came as a mercy to the worlds, and as one who unites all religions in Islam, which added to them what was added, of what the affairs of life and the developments of the age require, until the Hour is established.

Islam came as a purification for these people, whom they resumed with faith and resumed with righteous deeds, so for them is their full reward with their Lord; their former religion does not taint them, nor their corrupt and disbelieving creeds.

As for disagreement about prophethood, as the verse we are discussing mentions: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things (17)﴾ [al-Hajj]: judgment means that we know who is in the right and who is in the wrong. Thus the verses combined the situation of agreement and the situation of disagreement and explained the recompense of each of them.

So judgment is either a separation of places or a separation of recompenses. They said: naturally, the judgment between them, "this one is right and that one is wrong," will lead to different places and different recompenses.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things (17)﴾ [al-Hajj]: because Allah is the Judge who separates His servants, and a judge needs either evidence or witnesses, and witnesses must be upright, and uprightness in testimony is not realized except by a religion that prevents a person from deviating from the truth. But if the Judge is Allah, there is no need for evidence or witnesses, because His knowledge encompasses everything, and not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth escapes His knowledge.

It is remarkable that the judgment and separation from the Truth, glorified is He, encompass all authorities: legislative, judicial and executive. His judgment is not postponed, nor is it circumvented; rights are not lost in it as they are lost in the labyrinths and corridors of courts.

As for human judgment, legislation is separated from the judiciary, and the judiciary from execution, so a ruling may be issued while its execution is stalled; but the judgment of Allah is enforced, nothing postpones it.

Thus: the matter will not pass like this; rather, it is recorded for you or against you.

1 - Sabā yaṣbaʾu: he left one religion for another. The Sabians claim that they are upon the religion of Nuh (peace be upon him). It was said: they are worshippers of the angels. It was said: worshippers of the planets and stars. It was said: worshippers of fire. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/365).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 22, verse 18:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the creatures, and many of mankind? But many are deserving of punishment. And whoever Allah humiliates, there is none to honor him. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.﴾ (22:18)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen...﴾ (22:18). That is, "Do you not know?" Because the prostration of these things is prostration in its true sense, as we know prostration from ourselves, and each kind of existent has a prostration suited to it.

We have previously spoken about the kinds of existence, which are four: the lowest is the inanimate (jamad), then comes the plant (nabat), which adds the property of growth and the property of movement; then comes the animal (hayawan), which adds the property of sensation; then comes the human being, who adds the property of thought and choosing between alternatives.

Each of these kinds serves what is above it, and this circle ends with the fact that everything in Allah's creation is subjected to serve the human being. In a report: "O son of Adam, I created things for your sake, and I created you for My sake, so do not busy yourself with what is for you, neglecting the One for whom you are" (1).

So it was incumbent upon the human being to reflect on this distinction which his Lord has granted him, and to know that everything in existence, however small, has a task it performs and a role it fulfills. It is more fitting for you, O human, being the master of this universe, that you should have a task and a role in life, for you are no less than these creatures which Allah has subjected to you, otherwise you become less than them and lower.

If the task of all created things is to serve you because you are higher than them, then consider your task toward the One who is higher than you. When a messenger comes to you from one higher than you to alert you to this task, you must thank him, because he has alerted you to what you ought to occupy yourself with, and to Whom you must always be connected. Therefore the messenger is never to be turned away from, for he clarifies for you many matters that are the subject of rational inquiry.

The human intellect ought to reflect on all these kinds that serve it: Do you have power over them? Indeed they have served you since your childhood before you directed any command to them, and before you had the capacity to command or to make use of these things. You ought to have become aware of the power higher than you and than these creatures, the power that subjected the whole universe to your service. This is a natural inquiry that must arise.

These things, in their service to you, have never refused you, and have never failed you a single day. Look at the sun and the moon and others: Did the sun ever say one day: "These people do not deserve kindness, so I will not rise upon them today"?

The earth: Has it ever withheld from its planter one day? The wind: Has it ever ceased blowing? All of these are creatures stronger than you, over which you have no power, and you cannot subjugate them; rather they are in the grip of Allah, mighty and majestic, and subjected to you by His command, glorified is He. And because they are subjected, they never fail in performing their task.

As for the human being, corruption comes from him, and departure from obedience comes from him, because of the domain of choice which Allah has granted him.

Some say that the prostration of these creatures is a prostration of indication, not prostration in its true sense. But this view is contradicted by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Every one knows its prayer and its glorification...﴾ (24:41).

For every creature, however small, there is a prayer, glorification and prostration suited to its nature. If you reflect on human prostration with the forehead on the ground, you will find differences among people according to their states, though they are one kind: the prostration of the healthy person is not the prostration of the sick one who prostrates while on his bed or seated on a chair, and perhaps indicates with his eye or finger to signify prostration; if he cannot, he performs prostration in his heart.

If prostration varies in this way within a single kind according to its condition, capacity and strength, why do we find it unlikely that each kind has its own prostration suited to its nature?

And if this is the state of prostration in human beings, should we expect, for example, to see the prostration of the sun or the moon? Since the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, has said they prostrate, we must believe in their prostration, but in a manner known only to their Creator, exalted is He.

By Allah, if a sick person prays while seated on a chair or on a bed, do you, while he is in front of you, know that he is prostrating? So how do we hope to know the manner of the prostration of these creatures?

Among the meanings of prostration is submission and obedience. Whoever finds it unlikely that the prostration of these creatures is prostration in its true sense, let him take prostration here to mean submission, compliance and obedience, as you say of a proud person: "He came prostrating," meaning: humbled and abased. And from it is His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We have come willingly."﴾ (41:11)

So you may understand prostration in whichever of these meanings you wish, for you will not depart from His intent, glorified is He. And by the mercy of Allah He made these creatures submissive to His will; they never break free from it nor fail in it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and the human being bore it. Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant.﴾ (33:72)

Now we relate, and narrate, some dialogues of the wayfarers (al-salikin), the people of knowledge ('arifun) and the possessors of divine effusions (fuyudat), who understood from Allah and tasted the sweetness of His nearness, and who used to converse and compete not for vanity or boasting, but for advancement in nearness to Allah.

Two of these knowers sat together, and one of them had a mouthful of phlegm which he wished to spit out, and perplexity appeared on him as he looked here and there. His companion said to him: "Spit it out and be at ease." He said: "How, when every time I want to spit I hear the earth glorifying, so I am ashamed to cast it upon something that glorifies." The other said, and it seems he was of a higher rank than him, having feigned spitting: "A glorifier upon a glorifier."

So the people of unveiling (kashf) and the knowers of Allah perceive this glorification and acknowledge it, and according to the measure of knowledge of Allah you possess, and the understanding and perception you have, will be your reception and acceptance of such matters of faith.

And when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth...﴾ (22:18), it is known that those in the heavens are the angels, and we are not of them; but we are of the people of the earth, and the ruling of prostration encompasses us and we enter into its meaning. So why did He say after it: ﴿And many of mankind, and many are deserving of punishment...﴾ (22:18)?

The phrase ﴿And many of mankind; and many are deserving of punishment...﴾ (22:18) shows that we too have compulsion, subjection and prostration like the rest of the kinds of existence, and we also have a domain of choice. The disbeliever who is accustomed to rebelling against his Creator: he is commanded to believe and he disbelieves, commanded to obey and he disobeys. So why does he not rebel all the time? Why does he not refuse sickness if Allah afflicts him with it? And why does he not refuse death if it befalls him?

So the human being is commanded by the command of Allah like the tree, the stone and the animal, and the domain of choice is what gave rise to this division: many believed, and many are deserving of punishment.

But why did Allah, glorified and exalted is He, not make all creation subjected?

They said: because the attribute of subjection and of not departing from Allah's purposes establishes for Allah the attribute of power over all things, but it does not establish for Allah the attribute of being loved. Love exists only with choice: that you be free and choosing in believing or disbelieving, so you choose belief, and that you be free and able to disobey, yet you obey.

We give an example for this, and to Allah belongs the highest similitude: suppose you have two slaves; you tie one of them to you with a chain, and leave the other free. If you call to them both, they answer you. Which of them is more obedient to you: the compelled and forced one, or the free and unfettered one?

So subjection and compulsion establish power, and choice establishes love.

As for the difference that arose among people, that many of them believed and many of them are deserving of punishment, from where does this difference come, O Lord? From what You created in them of choice. Whoever wills may believe, and whoever wills may disbelieve. So the disbelief of the disbeliever and his choice are as if they were His, because Allah subjected him to choice, so even in his choice he is subjected.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And many of mankind...﴾ (22:18), that is: by their choices. It would have been expected that He say in contrast to it "and few," but these are many, and those are many too.

And the meaning of ﴿deserving of punishment...﴾ (22:18): "deserving" means established and confirmed. This is a matter that cannot be avoided, so that the believer and the disbeliever are not equal: ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ (68:35). So these must be punished, and the Truth requires that.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, there is none to honor him...﴾ (22:18). Because the entitlement to punishment comes from one equal to you; there may come one stronger than him who prevents it, or a intercessor who intercedes for him. But it is as if the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, despairs these people of being saved from His punishment, so no one will prevent them.

Whoever Allah wills to humiliate, no one will honor him, neither by granting him victory nor by intercession for him. So the meaning of ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates...﴾ (22:18) is: with the punishment that is deserved and confirmed for him. ﴿...there is none to honor him...﴾ (22:18): that is, to honor him and deliver him from this punishment. Likewise there is no one to exalt him, because exaltation can come only by compulsion against Allah, and that is impossible; or by an intercessor who intercedes for him with Allah, and no one intercedes with Allah except by His permission, glorified is He.

Therefore we say: the Truth, glorified is He, grants protection over His creation, and no one can seek protection against Him. That is, no one may say to Allah, "This one is under my protection." So He concluded the verse with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ (22:18).

1 – Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/228): it is reported in some divine books: Allah, exalted is He, says: "Son of Adam, I created you for My worship, so do not play; and I undertook your provision, so do not toil. Seek Me and you will find Me; if you find Me, you have found everything, and if you miss Me, you have missed everything, and I am more beloved to you than everything." Ahmad also narrated in his Musnad (2/358) from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "Allah said: Son of Adam, devote yourself to My worship and I will fill your heart with richness and close your poverty; and if you do not, I will fill your heart with preoccupation and not close your poverty."

Then the Truthful, Glorified One says:

﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them; boiling water will be poured over their heads.﴾ (22:19)

The word khasm (adversary, opponent) is one of those words that is used equally for the singular, the dual and the plural, and for the masculine and the feminine, as in His saying: ﴿Has the story of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the wall into the sanctuary?﴾ (38:21).

He also says: ﴿Two adversaries who have wronged one another...﴾ (38:22).

What is meant by His saying ﴿These two adversaries...﴾ (22:19) is His saying: ﴿And many among mankind, and many deserve the punishment...﴾ (22:18). Dispute requires a separation between the disputants, and separation requires witnesses. But if the separation comes from Allah, the Exalted, then no witnesses are needed: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ (4:79).

If He brings witnesses against them from among themselves, it is only to establish the proof against them and to rebuke them. He says: ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why have you testified against us?" They will say, "We were made to speak by Allah, who has made everything speak..."﴾ (41:21).

If you ask: how can the limbs testify against their owner on the Day of Resurrection when it is they who committed the deed?

We say: there is a difference between an act that I intend and an act that I merely carry out, and I may dislike it. For this, and to Allah belongs the highest comparison, let us take the example of a commander who orders his soldiers, and they must obey him even if the orders are wrong. If they return to the supreme commander and report what their commander did, that is because the supreme commander has given him authority over them and obliged them to obey him and to follow his command.

So the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, has given the human will authority over his limbs. The act, then, belongs to the will, and the limbs are merely instruments for execution. When you want, for example, to stand up, the moment you intend it you find yourself standing, without thinking about the movement of standing or the muscles that moved to perform this act, even though it is a complex process in which will, mind, nerves and organs cooperate, and you yourself feel none of this at all. Did you, in standing, order the limbs to move so that they moved?

If your limbs respond to you and obey you merely by your will, is it not more fitting that the creation of Allah should respond to the will of Allah?

Thus, the basis of actions is not the limbs but the will, as proof that when Allah wills to disable one of the limbs, He disables the commanding will and cuts it off from the limb, and then it is paralysed with no movement in it. If the person then wants to move it, he will not be able to. Why?

Because he does not know the parts that move this limb. If you asked the most knowledgeable people in the science of movement, and those who built robots: what is the mechanical movement that takes place in the human body so that he rises from his sleep or from his sitting? No one will be able to describe to you what takes place inside the body in this matter.

But if you looked, for example, at the excavator, which performs movements similar to those of the human body, you would find a boy operating it by using some buttons, and he can describe for you every movement in it and the machines that take part in each movement. So tell me, by Allah: which button do you press to move your hand or your arm? Which button do you move your eyes, your tongue, or your foot with? It is merely a will from you, and what you want responds to you, because Allah created you and gave your will complete control over your limbs. So do not consider it far-fetched that creatures should respond to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when He wills that they act.

Even the punishment in the Hereafter is not for these limbs and parts; the punishment is for the conscious self. This is shown by the fact that when a person is subjected to severe pain, he finds no relief from it except by sleeping, and when he awakes the pain returns to him. So it is the self that suffers and is tormented, not the limbs.

It is Allah, the Truthful, who will judge between these two adversaries, as He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection...﴾ (22:17).

Therefore the Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, said: "I will be the first to fall to his knees before the Lord on the Day of Resurrection for judgement, and with me 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith and Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. These are on one side, and on the opposite side: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah."

Why? Because between these men took place the first battle in Islam, and this was the first dispute that occurred in it. In the Battle of Badr, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out a group for single combat, and it was their custom in wars that the strongest and bravest of the people would come out for single combat, instead of the whole people being punished and everyone taking part in the fighting, exposing the lives of all people to danger.

Among this is what happened between Ali and Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with them both, at the battle of Siffin, when Ali said to Mu'awiyah: "Come out to me, O Mu'awiyah. If you defeat me, the matter is yours, and if I defeat you, the matter is mine." 'Amr ibn al-'As, who was in Mu'awiyah's ranks, said: "By Allah, O Mu'awiyah, the man has been fair to you," and in this lies the sparing of the blood of the Muslims on both sides.

Mu'awiyah looked at 'Amr and said: "By Allah, O 'Amr, you intended nothing but that I should go out to him so that he would kill me, and the matter would be yours after me. Since you have said what you said, let no one but you fight him. Go out to him."

So 'Amr stood up to fight Ali. But where is 'Amr from the courage and strength of Ali? Ali charged at 'Amr with a strong charge, and when 'Amr sensed that Ali would strike him a blow that would kill him, he resorted to a stratagem and used his cunning to turn Ali away from him: 'Amr uncovered his private parts, knowing full well that Ali would refrain from looking at the private parts. Indeed Ali left him and turned away, and 'Amr escaped by this trick of his.

The poet expressed this situation, saying:
"There is no good in warding off destruction with dishonour, as 'Amr warded it off one day by exposing his nakedness."

And al-Sharif al-Radi, who is of the Family of the Prophet's House, says in the qasida whose opening line is:
"Do I see you, whose eyes are tearful, with patience as your habit? Has love no command over you, nor any prohibition?
Indeed I am longing, and within me is a grief, but someone like me does not have his secret disclosed."
And in it he says:
"We are a people between whom there is no middle way: for us it is either the chest, before all people, or the grave."

Returning to Badr: when the disbelievers objected, after the Messenger of Allah brought out some men of the Ansar, they said: "These are obscure Ansar. We want you to bring out our equals from the men of Quraysh." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought out to them Ali, Hamzah and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and they brought out 'Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid. What happened was the victory of the Muslims and the defeat of the polytheists.

This is the day of which Allah said: ﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were humble. So fear Allah that you may be grateful.﴾ (3:123)

So Badr was a worldly separation between these two adversaries, and there remains the separation of the Hereafter, of which Imam Ali said: "I will be the first to fall to my knees before the Lord on the Day of Resurrection for judgement."

The meaning of ﴿they dispute concerning their Lord﴾ (22:19) is: that is, because of their difference concerning their Lord. One group believes in the existence of a god and another group denies him; one group affirms attributes for Him and another group negates these attributes. In other words, they divided into faith and disbelief.

Then He elaborates: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them; boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ (22:19).

﴿Garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ (22:19): it is as if the fire is tailored to the measure of their bodies, to make the punishment firm and to intensify it, so there is no looseness in it that could lessen its severity, and it is not loose-fitting on them.

Then ﴿boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾ (22:19). Al-hamim is water that has reached the limit of heat, so that it itself burns from the intensity of its heat. You may imagine water that our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has heated.

Thus Allah combines all kinds of punishment upon them, because a garment is worn by a person to cover his nakedness and protect him from heat and cold, so it encompasses the whole body. He says: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and at ease, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing.﴾ (16:112)

So the tasting is not in the garment; it is by something else. The garment gives encompassment and completeness, so that the tasting covers every part of the body and intensifies the punishment.

1 - Occasion of revelation of the verse: It is narrated from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to swear an oath that this verse, ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord...﴾ (22:19), was revealed concerning the three and the three who fought in single combat on the day of Badr, namely: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I will be the first to kneel in the dispute before the Lord on the Day of Resurrection." al-Wahidi cited it in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 176), and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/18) attributed it to al-Bukhari, Muslim and others.

2 - Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3733), who said: "I will be the first to kneel before the Compassionate for judgement on the Day of Resurrection." Qays ibn 'Abbad said: "Among them this verse was revealed, ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord...﴾ (22:19). They are those who fought in single combat on the day of Badr: Ali, Hamzah, 'Ubaydah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah."

3 - Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his book al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah (4/274) that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, called out: "Woe to you, O Mu'awiyah, come out to me and do not deceive me concerning what is between us." 'Amr ibn al-'As said to him: "Seize the opportunity, for he has already inflicted great slaughter by killing these four." Mu'awiyah said to him: "By Allah, you know well that Ali has never been defeated, and you only want to kill me so that you may obtain the caliphate after me. Go to him; someone like me is not deceived." It is also related that Ali once charged at 'Amr ibn al-'As and struck him with a spear, throwing him to the ground so that his private parts were exposed, and he turned away from him. His companions said: "What is the matter with you, O Commander of the Faithful, that you turned away from him?" He said: "Do you know what it was?" They said: "No." He said: "This is 'Amr ibn al-'As, who confronted me with his private parts, reminding me of the ties of kinship, so I turned away from him." When 'Amr returned to Mu'awiyah, the latter said to him: "Praise Allah, and praise your backside."

4 - He is Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, Abu'l-Hasan al-Radi al-'Alawi al-Husayni, the most eloquent poet of the Talibids. Born in 359 AH and died (406 AH) in Baghdad. The leadership of the nobility (naqabat al-ashraf) came to him during his father's lifetime. His works include "al-Majazat al-Nabawiyyah," "Majaz al-Qur'an," and "Khasa'is Amir al-Mu'minin Ali ibn Abi Talib" (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 6/99).

5 - Mentioned by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (2/625) that 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah came out between his brother Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah and his son al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, until when he stepped out of the line he called for single combat. Young men from the Ansar, three in number, came out to him: 'Awf and Mu'awwidh, the two sons of al-Harith, whose mother was 'Afra', and another man said to be 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah. They said: "Who are you?" They said: "A group of the Ansar." They said: "We have no need of you." Then their herald called out: "O Muhammad, bring out to us our equals from our people." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Stand up, O 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, stand up, O Hamzah, stand up, O Ali." When they stood and approached them, they said: "Who are you?" They replied: "Noble equals." 'Ubaydah, who was the oldest of the group, fought 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah; Hamzah fought Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah; and Ali fought al-Walid ibn 'Utbah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 20:

﴿Whereby that which is in their bellies and their skins will be melted.﴾

We have said that this water has reached the utmost of heat, so it does not boil at the degree of heat that we know. Rather, it is brought to boil by its Lord, Whom no one can endure His punishment. When you pour boiling water over a person's body, it scalds his body from the outside, but it does not reach his inside. But this water, when it is poured over them, melts what is in their bellies first, then their skins after that. So, O Allah, protect us from Your punishment on the day You resurrect Your servants.

﴿And for them are maces of iron.﴾ (22:21)

Al-Maqami' (the maces, or goads): these are the whips with which a beast is subdued and restrained so that it submits to you, or with which a person is punished when you chastise him. But they are whips of iron, and so they indicate humiliation and abasement, in addition to the torment.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, explains the function of these hooks (al-maqami').

﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, out of anguish, they will be returned into it, and it will be said, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾

Allah, glorified and exalted, depicts the state of the people of the Fire, what they are in of punishment, and of despair that it will be lightened for them. When they try to escape the anguish of the punishment, these whips come to them and return them to where they were. A person may become accustomed to a kind of torment, so the matter becomes easier for him. For example, the prisoner who is beaten with whips on his back: after a number of blows he loses feeling, and no blow after that affects him.

Al-Mutanabbi(1) excelled in describing this meaning when he said:

"Fate has struck me with calamities until
I am as if in a covering of arrows.
So when arrows struck me, the points
were broken upon the points."

But how can it be lightened for the people of the Fire, when Allah, glorified and exalted, says:
﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will exchange them for other skins, that they may taste the punishment...﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:56].

In their being returned there is despair for them after they had hoped for deliverance, and how severe is despair after hope upon the soul. Therefore they say: "No calamity is more grievous than the despair of one who is hooked, after the hope of one who is hooked."

As He, the Exalted, says:
﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass that scalds the faces...﴾ [Al-Kahf 18:29]. At the moment they hear the relief they hope and rejoice, then despair comes to them in ﴿water like molten brass that scalds the faces...﴾ [Al-Kahf 18:29].

As for His saying, ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [Al-Hajj 22:22]: al-hariq (the burning) is that which burns other things by its intensity.

Since the verses spoke of the disbelievers and the punishment that befell them, it was necessary to speak of the opposite, of the believers, so that the intellect might draw a comparison between this and that. The believer becomes more steadfast in faith and more averse to disbelief, and likewise the disbeliever becomes aware of the consequence of his disbelief, renounces it and returns to faith. Thus everyone benefits from this contrast, and it is as if Allah, glorified and exalted, gives us, in the verses of the Qur'an and in these contrasts, the means of salvation and mercy.

1 - Al-Mutanabbi: he is Ahmad ibn al-Husayn Abu al-Tayyib al-Kindi. He was born in 303 AH in Kufa, in a quarter called Kinda. He grew up in Syria, then moved through the desert seeking literature and the science of Arabic. He composed poetry as a youth, and claimed prophethood in the desert of al-Samawa. The governor of Homs captured him and imprisoned him until he repented and retracted his claim. He died in 354 AH at the age of 52 (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/115).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 23:

إن الله يدخل الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار يحلون فيها من أساور من ذهب ولؤلؤا ولباسهم فيها حرير ( ٢٣ ) } :

Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow; therein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk. (22:23)

The Almighty and Glorious says:

Allah, the Exalted, makes clear what He has prepared for His believing servants: the dwelling, ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ (22:23); the adornment, ﴿therein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ (22:23); and the clothing, ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ (22:23). Thus He has gathered for them the bliss of dwelling, adornment and clothing.

In the Hereafter, men will enjoy silk and gold, which were forbidden to them in this world. Here some women may object: "Where is the bliss in something we enjoyed in this world, namely silk and gold?"

Yes, you (women) enjoy silk and gold in this world. But in the Hereafter it is another kind, and a complete enjoyment that nothing spoils. Jewelry for a woman is pure, free of impurities, and lasting with her; no one takes it from her, and she does not need to change it or sell it, for it renews itself in her hand every day, so she sees it in a new craftsmanship and a new form different from what it was.(1) As we said earlier, in His saying about the people of Paradise: ﴿They will say, "This is what we were provided with before." (2:25)﴾

So they assume that the food and fruit of Paradise are like the fruit of the world which they ate before. Therefore their Lord explains to them that it is not like the fruit of the world: ﴿and they will be given it in resemblance (mutashabihan) (2:25)﴾, meaning: different varieties within a single kind.

1 - Ibn al-Qayyim (in Hadi al-Arwah, p. 189) cited from Ka'b al-Ahbar, as related by Ibn Abi al-Dunya: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has an angel since the day He created (the world) who fashions the jewelry of the people of Paradise until the Hour arrives. If a single piece of the jewelry of Paradise were brought out, it would overshadow the light of the sun's rays. So do not ask after this about the jewelry of Paradise."

Then the Truth says:

﴿And they were guided to good speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (24).﴾

(They were guided): Allah guided them. The One who showed them the means of entering Paradise and of enjoying in it dwelling, adornment and clothing, likewise guides them now in Paradise and shows them how to thank the Bestower for this blessing. This is the meaning of: ﴿And they were guided to good speech (24)﴾ [al-Hajj]. This good speech is summarized by other verses, among them His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us (74)﴾ [az-Zumar].

And His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty (35)﴾ [Fatir].

And His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief (34)﴾ [Fatir].

So when the people of Paradise enter Paradise and enjoy lasting bliss, they can only say: "Praise be to Allah," as the Truth, glorified is He, says of them: ﴿And their final call will be: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds (10)﴾ [Yunus].

And they (the scholars) said: ﴿The good speech (24)﴾ [al-Hajj] is the word of tawhid: "There is no god but Allah." This word is the beloved one that brought us to Paradise. The meaning encompasses every good speech, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Have you not seen how Allah sets forth a parable: a good word like a good tree, its root firmly fixed and its branches in the sky (24)﴾ [Ibrahim].

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (24)﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, Allah guided them to the way of Paradise, or to Paradise itself, as He said in another verse about the disbelievers: ﴿Nor will He guide them to a path (168) except the path of Hell... (169)﴾ [an-Nisa'].

1 - Ibn 'Abbas said this, saying: He means "There is no god but Allah" and "Praise be to Allah." (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4562). Abu al-'Aliyah said: their saying "Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector" — that is, in dispute. Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid said: the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: sincerity (ikhlas). 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except through Allah." (al-Durr al-Manthur 6/24).

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar (others) from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque, which We have made (equally) for the people, the resident therein and the visitor (equal). And whoever intends therein deviation (from the right) with injustice - We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾ (22:25):

The verses have moved us to a new subject: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve...﴾ [al-Hajj] is in the past tense, because disbelief has occurred from them as an actual act. ﴿...and bar...﴾ [al-Hajj] is in the present tense. The expected form would be "kafaru wa-sadduu" (they disbelieved and barred), but the matter is not a rigid rule nor a mechanical procedure, because their barring from the way of Allah arises from disbelief, and their barring is still continuing.

The meaning of ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj]: that is, from jihad. ﴿And the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj]: because they prevented the Muslims from entering it, while it was in their grip and under their control. This indeed happened at al-Hudaybiyah, when the companions of the Messenger of Allah longed to perform the 'umrah and to circumambulate the House, from which they had been deprived for a long time. When they set out, the disbelievers of Makkah prevented them and barred them from entering it.

﴿And the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj]: the word "haram" (sacred, inviolable) indicates that it is forbidden to commit a wrong in it, to disrespect it, or to transgress within it. The word "al-haram" describes some places and some times, and there are five things: we say the Sacred House, which is the Ka'bah; the Sacred Mosque; the Sacred Land (al-balad al-haram), meaning Makkah; then the Sacred Monument (al-mash'ar al-haram). These are concentric circles centred on the Ka'bah; these are places. The fifth is a time: the sacred months, concerning which Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting therein...﴾ [al-Baqarah] (2:217).

The sanctity of time and place here is for a wisdom intended by the Creator, the Almighty, since He is a Lord merciful to His creation, wishing to give them an opportunity to conceal their pride and to restrain their arrogance. Wars and conflicts used to spread among the people, kindled by tribal customs and the frenzy of war, to the extent that each of the two sides wished to annihilate the other, and they might continue in war while hating it, but their pride would prevent them from retreating and withdrawing.

Therefore Allah, the Almighty, made sanctity for these places and times, to be a screen for this false pride and this hateful honour. Every event needs a time and a place. So Allah forbade fighting in the sacred months, so that when war flared up among them, a sacred month would come and rescue the weak from the grip of the strong without wounding his pride, and perhaps he would shake his head saying: "Had it not been for the sacred month, I would have done to them such and such."

So this, then, is a mercy from Allah to His servants, and a screen that protects them from the evils of their own selves and their impulses, and preserves their blood.

The pride of the Arabs in this matter resembles the pride of a couple who quarrel reluctantly, each wanting the other to come to him, but his pride prevents him from yielding. The man sat in his room and closed the door upon himself. The wife looked, and there he was raising his hands, praying to Allah that his wife would reconcile with him. So she went and adorned herself for him, then pushed the door upon him and said, as though someone were forcing her to enter: "Mudiyani fin ya Umm Hashim" (Take me, where are you, O Umm Hashim).

Likewise, a place was made sacred, because the sacred time in which fighting is forbidden is four months: three consecutive and one single. The single one is Rajab, and the consecutive are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram.

So He also forbade fighting in these places, to protect the blood of creatures from being shed because of tribal strife arising from rancour, hatred, pride and arrogance.

Allah, the Exalted, says concerning the prohibition of fighting at the Sacred Mosque: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ (2:191) [al-Baqarah].

Perhaps when the months of prohibition come, or when they reach its place, they rest from war, and so they realise the pleasure of peace and the importance of reconciliation, and they resolve the causes of dispute between them without war. The frenzy of war drags on war, while the pleasure of peace, the comfort of security, and the feeling of the calm of life draw an inclination towards reconciliation and the settlement of such disputes by peaceful means.

The one who reflects on these places which Allah has made sacred finds them in ranks, as though they were concentric circles centred on the House of Allah, the Sacred, which is the Ka'bah; then the Sacred Mosque around it; then the Sacred Land, which is Makkah; then the Sacred Monument, which takes only a part of time, in the days of Hajj.

As for the Ka'bah, it is not, as some suppose, this structure that we see. The Ka'bah is the place, and this structure is the one who occupies it. So if you were to demolish this building that stands now, the place of the building is the House, its place whether you descend into the depths of the earth or ascend through the layers of the heavens.

Thus the Sacred House of Allah is this tract of earth extending up to the sky. Do you not see people praying on the upper floors, who are far higher than this building? They face the air above the Ka'bah, not the Ka'bah itself. Why? Because the Ka'bah extends into the air as far as Allah wills.

Next comes the Mosque, which is a piece of land dedicated to being a mosque. But there is a mosque by place when you establish it and make for it a building such as this building in which we are speaking now, and it is called a "mosque" by place. Or a mosque by occupant, when this mosque becomes too narrow for us and we go out to pray in the street; in this case it is a mosque. They said: even if it extended to Sana'a and the rows were joined, all of it would be a mosque.

We return to what took place between the Muslims and the polytheists on the day of al-Hudaybiyah. The disbelievers barred the Muslims from the House of Allah while they were within sight of it, so the Muslims were enraged by that, and some of them saw fit to enter Makkah by force, against their will.

But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a secret between himself and his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, so he accepted their conditions and concluded with them a treaty, the "Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah", which stirred the indignation of the companions, foremost among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. He said to the Messenger of Allah: "O Messenger of Allah, are we not upon the truth?" He (ﷺ) said: "Yes." He said: "Are they not upon falsehood?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why should we accept the humiliation in our religion?" (3)

Among the terms of this treaty: if a disbeliever embraces Islam and joins the ranks of the Muslims, Muhammad (ﷺ) would return him, and if a Muslim goes to them, they would not return him to the Muslims (4).

The Mother of the Believers, Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, had a great stance in this hardship, and a sound opinion that brought the opinions of the men back to guidance and to what is correct.
