This is something we take pride in regarding women in Islam, and by it we answer those who loudly claim the rights of women.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to his tent angry, he said to Umm Salamah: "The Muslims are ruined, O Umm Salamah. I commanded them, but they did not comply." He meant: he had commanded them to return without performing the 'umrah this year.

The Mother of the Believers said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are distressed, for they have been prevented from the House of Allah while they are within sight of it. But go, O Messenger of Allah, to what your Lord has commanded you, and do it. When they see you do it, they will know that the matter is final" — meaning there is no going back on it. Indeed, the Messenger of Allah took this advice, went and shaved his head, slaughtered his offering, and the people did likewise, and this matter ended (5).

But before they returned to Madinah, Allah's will decided to inform them of the wisdom in the Messenger of Allah's acceptance of the conditions of the polytheists, even though they were unjust and oppressive conditions.

First: in this treaty and this pact there is a recognition by them of Muhammad, his standing and his rank, and that he had become their equal, and this is a gain in itself.

Second: both parties agreed to cease fighting between them for a number of years, and this period gave the Muslims an opportunity to devote themselves to receiving delegations and spreading the religion of Allah.

Third: it was within the power of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to enter Makkah against the will of its people, and it was within his capacity to kill them all. But what would have been the position of the believers regarding the people of Makkah, among whom were those who concealed their faith and whom no one knew? They were among these disbelievers, and what befalls the disbelievers would befall them. Had the believers been distinguished from the disbelievers, or had they come out on one side, it would have been possible to avoid them.

Read His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering detained from reaching its place. And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby be struck with blame without knowledge - (so that) Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills. If they had been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment.﴾ (48:25) [al-Fath].

Then He, the Exalted, says concerning the Sacred Mosque: ﴿That which We have made for the people...﴾ [al-Hajj] — that is, all of them — ﴿...equal, the resident therein and the visitor﴾ [al-Hajj]. "The resident therein" means the one who stays there, and "the visitor" means the one who comes to it from outside Makkah. The meaning of ﴿equal﴾ [al-Hajj] is that these two categories are completely equal.

Therefore we say to those who reserve places for their own accounts in the Sacred House of Allah in particular, and in the houses of Allah in general: relax yourselves. The place is reserved with Allah for whoever precedes, not for whoever places his prayer mat and occupies the place with it.

This verse ﴿equal, the resident therein and the visitor﴾ [al-Hajj] has prompted some to say that it is not permissible to rent houses in Makkah; whoever wishes to stay in a house may stay in it without rent, so that the resident and the stranger are equal (7).

This opinion is refuted by the fact that houses are a place and an occupied dwelling. The land of Makkah was for everyone when the place was free, where whoever wished could build. But once a person builds a house and lives in it, he becomes its occupant, and it is not permissible for anyone to enter it except with his permission and will.

This question was debated between al-Hanzali in Makkah and Imam al-Shafi'i (10), where al-Hanzali held that it is not permissible to rent houses in Makkah, because according to this verse they belong to everyone. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, replied: "If it were so, He would not have said, concerning the emigrants: ﴿those who were expelled from their homes...﴾ [al-Hashr] (59:8).

He attributed the homes to them. And when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: 'Has 'Aqil left us any house or any dwelling?' (11) And 'Aqil selling their houses after they emigrated is evidence of their ownership of them." Therefore al-Hanzali returned to the opinion of al-Shafi'i.

This is although the verse refers only to the House, not to all of Makkah, so the disagreement would not have extended to the whole of Makkah.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with injustice - We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾ (22:25) [al-Hajj]: deviation may occur in the highest right, which is deviation regarding Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But here what is meant by deviation is turning away from the path of truth. His saying ﴿with injustice﴾ [al-Hajj]: injustice in a matter does not ascend to the level of disbelief, and deviation with injustice, if it occurs in the House of Allah, is a grave matter, because you are in the house of your Lord (the Ka'bah).

You ought to be ashamed of even merely entertaining sin in the soul. Mere intention here counts as a sin, because you are in a station in which you must feel awe and reverence. Just as Allah has given His House a distinction in multiplying good deeds, so too the matter of disobedience is magnified while you are in the precincts of His House. So be mindful of this matter (12).

Even in the sayings of country folk they say: "You come into the house of the scholar and get drunk." That is, drunkenness is conceivable in the house of one of the sinners, in a tavern or a house of a profligate; but in the house of a scholar, this is a great thing and a tremendous audacity. Why?

For the place has sanctity by the sanctity of its owner. If the place has sanctity by the sanctity of its owner, and the House is attributed to Allah, then you are disobeying your Lord in His very abode, and what greater audacity is there than audacity against Allah?

This is a special quality of the Sacred Mosque. Every mosque anywhere is a house of Allah, but there is a difference between a house of Allah by the choice of Allah and a house of Allah by the choice of the servants of Allah. Therefore the house of Allah by the choice of Allah (the Sacred House) is the qiblah towards which all the houses of Allah on earth turn.

What is the consequence of deviation in the house of Allah? ﴿We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [al-Hajj]: they will taste the punishment by the command of the Truth, always and forever. Tasting is the most powerful of perceptions, and that is the humiliating punishment. Tasting is the sensation of what is eaten, whether drink or food, but it has extended beyond every thing perceived by taste, even if it is not something eaten or drunk. Our Lord, the Mighty and Generous, says: ﴿Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the generous﴾ (44:49) [al-Dukhan].

Notes:

And Abu Bakr said to him: 'O son of al-Khattab, he is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never waste him.'"
4 - The view of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this condition that Quraysh stipulated was what he said: "Whoever comes to them from us, may Allah banish him; and whoever comes to us from them, we shall return him to them; Allah will grant him relief and a way out." 6 - Law tazayyalu: law tafarraqu (if they had separated), as stated by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, as transmitted from him by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari (mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 7/534).
7 - al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (6/4564): "Their houses were without doors until theft increased, so a man made a door, and 'Umar objected to him and said: 'Will you lock a door in the face of the pilgrims to the House of Allah?' The man said: 'I only wanted to protect their goods from theft.' So he left it, and people then made doors. It is narrated from Malik that houses are not like the mosque, and their occupants have the right to refuse entry and to exclusive use. This is the practice today, and this is the view of the majority of the imams."
8 - Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/21): this is the question on which al-Shafi'i and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh disagreed at Masjid al-Khayf, while Ahmad ibn Hanbal was also present, and he mentioned the argument of each of them.
9 - He is Ishaq ibn Rahawayh Abu Ya'qub al-Hanzali, resident and scholar of Nishapur, born in 161 AH, one of the great memorisers of hadith. Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and others took from him. Hadith, jurisprudence, memorisation, truthfulness and asceticism were combined in him (al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 1/292; Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 2/433).

Born in 150 AH in Gaza, Palestine, and taken to Makkah when he was two years old. He visited Baghdad twice and went to Egypt in 199 AH, where he died; his grave is well known in Cairo. 'Aqil had inherited from Abu Talib, he and Talib, and Ja'far and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, inherited nothing from him, because they were Muslims, while 'Aqil and Talib were disbelievers."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 26:

﴿And [remember] when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ (22:26):

Since the preceding discussion concerned the Sacred House, it is appropriate to speak of its history and its construction. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And [remember] when We settled Abraham at the site of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ [al-Hajj]. The meaning of baww'a (بوأ) is: He made it a mubā'a (مباءة), i.e., a place to which one goes for his work and his needs, and then returns to it and comes back, like a home to which a person returns. Among its uses is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they returned with anger from Allah...﴾ (2:61) [al-Baqarah].

Idh (إذ) is a temporal adverb referring to an event after which the report of that event follows. The meaning is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Remember, O Muhammad, the time when it was said to Abraham such-and-such." Thus, in every verse of the Qur'an, idh comes in an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning an event that occurred at that time.

But what is the connection between the mubā'a, or the place one settles in, and the matter of the House? They say: because the settled place is a piece of land chosen by a person to return to from the hardships of his life, and a person does not choose such a place unless all the essentials of life are available in it.

Therefore the Exalted says in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed...﴾ (12:56) [Yusuf].

And He said concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement...﴾ (10:93) [Yunus]. So the meaning of ﴿We settled Abraham at the site of the House...﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj] is: We made it a mubā'a for him, to which he returns from the movement of his life, after We had informed him and guided him to its place.(1)

We have said that the makān (مكان, place) is not the same as the makīn (مكين, the one who dwells). The makān is the spot in which the makīn occupies and settles. So the ground of this mosque is a makān, and the structure standing on this ground is called "a makīn in this makān." On this basis, Allah guided Abraham, peace be upon him, to the place where He would command him to establish the House.

The scholars have had lengthy discussion on this matter. Some hold that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first to build the House. We say to the proponents of this view: Allah, blessed and exalted is He, settled Abraham at the site of the House, meaning He showed it to him, as if the House already existed. The proof is that Allah says in the story, on the tongue of Abraham: ﴿Indeed, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House...﴾ (14:37) [Ibrahim].

And in His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael...﴾ (2:127) [al-Baqarah].

It is known that Ishmael shared in the building with his father and assisted him when he grew up and became able to help his father. As for the settling, it was when Ishmael was still an infant. His saying, ﴿near Your sacred House...﴾ (14:37) [Ibrahim], indicates that the "nearness" existed before Ishmael reached the age to help his father build the House. Hence this is evidence that the House existed before Abraham.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has clarified this matter in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾ (3:96) [Al 'Imran].

So that we agree on the understanding of the verse, we ask: who are "mankind"? Mankind are Adam and his descendants until the Hour arrives. Thus Adam is among mankind, so why would the generality of the verse not include him? The House was established for mankind, and Adam is among mankind, so it must have been established for Adam too.

Therefore one may say that the House was established even before Adam. Accordingly, we accept the opinion that the angels were the first to establish the House; then the Flood obliterated its landmarks, so Allah guided Abraham, by revelation from Him, to the place of the House, and commanded him to raise it anew in this valley.

It is also said that Allah sent to Abraham a cloud that guided him to the place and spoke: "O Abraham, take the measure by My measure," meaning the construction.(2)

If you reflect on the meaning of ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House...﴾ (2:127) [al-Baqarah]: al-raf' (الرفع) means elevation, which is the third dimension. It is as if the foundations already had a real length and width, and Abraham had to raise them.

But why did Allah settle Abraham at the site of the House?

When Abraham settled his descendants near the House, he said: ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer...﴾ (14:37) [Ibrahim]. It is as if the matter from its beginning was a matter of worship and establishing prayer, prayer to the true God and the Lord of truth. Therefore He first commanded him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj]. The meaning is: purify this place from everything that suggests association with others, for this is the correct beginning for establishing the House of Allah.

Would it be conceivable that Abraham, peace be upon him, fell into association? Certainly not; Abraham was far removed from shirk. But when Allah sends a messenger, he is the first to receive the commands from Allah in order to convey them to his people; he is the first to receive and the first to implement, so that he may be an example to his people, so that they believe him and trust him, for he has commanded them with a matter from which he is not exempt.

Do you not see His saying to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah...﴾ (33:1) [al-Ahzab]? Did Muhammad (ﷺ) deviate from the fear of Allah? Rather, the command is directed at the community in the person of its messenger, so that the matter becomes easy for us when our Lord commands us to fear Him, and we do not see any indignity in this command which the Messenger of Allah preceded us in. You will notice that some people feel too proud to say to someone, "O so-and-so, fear Allah," and perhaps regard it as an insult and an accusation, thinking it is said only to one who has done something contrary to piety.

This is a mistaken understanding of the command to piety. When I say to you, "Fear Allah," it does not mean that I deny you piety; rather I remind you to begin the movement of your life with the fear of Allah.

Therefore His saying to Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿that you not associate anything with Me...﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj] does not mean the imagining that shirk occurred from Abraham. And He said ﴿anything﴾ (shay'an) so that the prohibition includes every kind of shirk, whatever its form: a tree, a stone, an idol, stars, or planets.

This meaning is affirmed by His saying: ﴿and purify My House...﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj]. Purification means moral purity by removing the causes of shirk and making worship sincerely for Allah alone without partner, and sensory purity from what had befallen it through the passage of time and the occurrence of the Flood, for there may be some filth on it, for example.

The meaning of ﴿for those who circumambulate...﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj] is those who go around the House. ﴿and those who stand...﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj] means those who remain and seclude themselves in it for worship. ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾ (22:26) [al-Hajj] means those who go to it at the times of the prayers to perform the prayer. Prayer is expressed by bowing and prostration because they are the most evident acts of prayer.

1 - That is, We showed him its origin so that he could clarify it, for it had been effaced by the Flood and other things. When the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, came, Allah commanded him to build it. He came to its location and began to search for a trace, so Allah sent a wind that uncovered the foundation of Adam, peace be upon him, and he arranged its foundations upon it. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4567).

2 - al-Daylami related from Ali, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House...﴾ (2:127) [al-Baqarah], that he said: a cloud came upon the square of the House, having a head that spoke: "The height of the House is on my square," so they raised it upon its square. (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1/307).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 27:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, coming from every deep mountain pass.﴾ (22:27)

After Allah had raised the foundations of the House, He commanded His Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to proclaim the pilgrimage among the people. Why? Because the House is the House of Allah, and all creatures are the creation of Allah. So why should the sight of the House be limited to those whom it was decreed to pass by it, or to live beside it?

Al-Haqq (the Truth), glory be to Him and exalted is He, wished to spread this distinction among all His creatures, so that they would go to see the House of their Lord. Although all mosques are the houses of Allah, this particular House is the House of Allah by Allah's own choosing. For this reason He made it the qibla (direction of prayer) for the houses that people choose.

Among the signs of loyalty between people is that we visit the palaces of great men and dignitaries, and the visitor signs his name in the visitors' register, seeing in that honour and elevation. So what of the House of Allah? How could its visiting and sight be limited to its people and neighbours, or to those for whom it was decreed that they pass by it?

The meaning of ﴿proclaim﴾ (22:27) is: the adhan (call) is knowledge, and the first means of knowledge is hearing with the ear, and from "ear" (udhn) the adhan is derived, meaning announcement. From this same root is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ (14:7), meaning: made known. The ear is the first means of hearing and the initial address through which we learn; therefore, before you speak, you must hear.

When Allah commanded Ibrahim to proclaim, there was none around the House except Ibrahim, his son and his wife. So to whom would he proclaim? And who would listen in a vast, boundless desert and an uninhabited valley? So his Lord called to him: "O Ibrahim, upon you is the proclamation, and upon Us is the delivery."(2)

Your task is to raise your voice with the adhan; upon Us is delivering this call to all people, in every age and in every place. Mankind, all of them, will hear it, both those in the world of the atoms (dhar) and those in the loins of their fathers,(3) by the power of Allah, the Exalted, who said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ (8:17).

That is to say: Perform what is upon you, and leave what is beyond your capacity to the power of your Lord. Ibrahim proclaimed the pilgrimage among the people, and the call reached all mankind until the Hour is established. Whoever responds and answers, saying "Labbayka Allahumma labbayk" (Here I am, O Allah, here I am), a pilgrimage is recorded for him. Some scholars have said:(4) whoever answers once, a pilgrimage is recorded for him; whoever answers twice, two pilgrimages are recorded for him, and so on, because the meaning of labbayk is: a response to You after a response.

If you say: the demands and commands of Allah are many, so why has the Hajj in particular received this status? We say: the pillars of Islam begin with the two testimonies: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," then prayer, then zakat, then fasting, then Hajj. If you look at these pillars, you will find that Hajj is the only pillar for which a Muslim strives to perform it even if he is not able to, so you see him saving and economising, even from his sustenance, and perhaps depriving himself in order to perform the obligation of Hajj. This does not happen, and a person does not undertake it, except in this obligation. Why?

They said: because Allah, the Exalted, has decided in this matter, saying: "proclaim… they will come to you," in such a way that it is against their will and without their choice. Do you not see people being drawn to perform this obligation, as if a force outside themselves were pulling them?

This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them﴾ (14:37). The meaning of "incline" (tahwi) is: to come without choice, from hawy, meaning falling, which is something a person does not control, like one who falls from a high place, having no choice in not falling.

Thus hearts yearn for the House of Allah and move with longing towards it, as if something were drawing them to perform this obligation, because Allah, the Exalted, commanded this obligation and decreed it by His words ﴿they will come to you﴾ (22:27). As for other matters, He commanded them and left them to the choice of the one bound by the command, who either obeys or disobeys. So this matter is a true decree by the text of the Qur'an.

Some people of understanding say: the command in ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾ (22:27) is not addressed to Ibrahim, but to Muhammad (ﷺ), the one upon whom the Qur'an was revealed, and this verse addresses him. So the meaning is: "Remember, O you upon whom My Book was revealed, when We settled Ibrahim in the place of the House" (22:26). That is, remember this matter, ﴿and proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾ (22:27). So the command here is as if it were addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ).(5)

Therefore we do not see this rite among other nations, such as the Jews and Christians. They do not perform Hajj and never go to the House of Allah. It is established that Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, performed Hajj to the House of Allah,(6) but it is not established that Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, performed Hajj. The proof is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is about to happen that the son of Maryam (Mary) will descend, and he will come for Hajj, visit my grave, and be buried there."(7)

The Messenger said, "and he will come for Hajj," because he has not died, and he will reach the period of obligation from the Messenger when he descends from heaven, and he will pray behind an imam from the community of Muhammad, may Allah's blessings be upon all of His prophets and messengers.

Among the matters we argue against them is their saying that the one who was sacrificed was Ishaq (Isaac). For if the one sacrificed were Ishaq, as they claim, then the rites of sacrifice, the ransom, and the stoning of the jamarat would be with you in Syria. But these rites are here in Makkah, where Isma'il was.

Then remember carefully what your Holy Book(8) says in chapters 23 and 24: that the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, revealed to Ibrahim that he should ascend a mountain of Paran and take his only son, Isma'il, not Ishaq, because Allah ransomed Isma'il, and then gave Ibrahim the good news of Ishaq.

It is part of the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic, that He placed in the lie of the liar an opening for the truth, and cracks through which we reach the reality. For this reason, the men of the judiciary say: there is no perfect crime at all; the criminal must leave some indication that points to him, however careful he is with his crime, such as something falling from him, even a button from his clothes, or a small paper with a telephone number, and so on. So we say: crime does not benefit, for the criminal will inevitably fall into the hands of the one who will exact retribution from him.

Judges and public prosecutors have great ability to extract the truth from the very mouths of criminals. The judge keeps conversing with him until he finds in his speech a gap or a contradiction through which he reaches the truth.

This is because truth has only one face, and its speaker cannot falter or hesitate, whereas falsehood has more than one face, and the liar himself, if you converse with him more than once, you will find change and contradiction in his speech. For this reason, the Arabs say: "If you are a liar, then be a good memoriser" (kun dhakuran), meaning: remember what you said first, so that you do not change it afterwards.

Among the examples of lies that expose their speaker is when one says to another: "Do you remember the day we were in such-and-such a place on the night of the little Eid, and the moon was like noon?" He replied: "How can the moon be like noon at the end of the month?"

The judge may resort to some stratagems, and must use his intelligence to clarify the face of the truth. For example, a judge to whom two men came for judgment, one of whom accused the other of taking his money as a trust, then taking it for himself and burying it in such-and-such a place. When the judge conversed with the accused, he denied it, so the judge turned away from him and went to the owner of the trust, saying to him: "Go to this place and search; perhaps you forgot it here or there."

Or perhaps someone else took it from you. The owner of the money went off. Suddenly the judge asked the accused: "Why has so-and-so been delayed all this time?" The accused replied: "Because the place is far away, Your Honour the judge." His memory betrayed him, and he uttered the truth without realising it.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿they will come to you on foot﴾ (22:27). The word "rijalan" (on foot) here is not the plural of rajul (man), but the plural of rajil, which is one who walks on his feet. ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ (22:27): the dhamir (lean one) is a horse or camel made thin from the length of the journey.

Placing those on foot before those riding is an affirmation of the divine command, ﴿they will come to you﴾ (22:27): everyone is eager to perform the obligation, even if one performs Hajj on foot.

As for His words, ﴿coming from every deep mountain pass﴾ (22:27): that is, from every wide road; ﴿deep﴾ (22:27) means far away.

1 - Ad-dhamir: slender of body, with little flesh. It is the custom of the Arabs to train horses (yudmir al-khayl) so that they become stronger, more active and faster. The Exalted's words ﴿and on every lean camel﴾ (22:27) mean a lean horse accustomed to long journeys with vigour and strength (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/395).

2 - From Ibn Abbas, who said: When Ibrahim finished building the House, he said: "My Lord, I have finished." Then He said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage…﴾ (22:27). He said: "My Lord, and how will my voice reach?" He said: "Proclaim, and upon Me is the delivery." He said: "My Lord, how should I say it?" He said: "O people, the Hajj to the Ancient House has been prescribed for you." So it was heard from between the heaven and the earth. Do you not see that they come from the farthest part of the earth, answering (labbayk)? Recorded by al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (6/32), attributing it to Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*.

3 - From Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage…﴾ (22:27), he said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, stood on the stone and called: "O people, the Hajj has been prescribed. So hear, whoever is in the loins of men and the wombs of women." Whoever believed among those who had been predestined in Allah's knowledge to perform Hajj until the Day of Resurrection answered: "Labbayk Allah, labbayk." Recorded by al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (6/33), attributing it to Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

4 - Recorded by al-Daylami in *al-Firdaws bi-ma'thur al-khitab* (no. 5303) from Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Suyuti said in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (6/33): "Recorded by al-Daylami with a very weak chain, from Ali, raised (to the Prophet)." Al-Fatani said in *Tadhkirat al-Mawdu'at* (p. 73): "The hadith is from the copy of Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath, most of whose hadiths are munkar (rejected)."

5 - Al-Qurtubi said in his *Tafsir* (6/4569): "It has been said: the address to Ibrahim was completed at His words ﴿and the bowing and prostrating﴾ (22:26). Then Allah, mighty and majestic, addressed Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage…﴾ (22:27)."

6 - From Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by the valley of al-Azraq and said: "What valley is this?" They said: "This is the valley of al-Azraq." He said: "As if I were looking at Musa (peace be upon him) descending from the pass, with wailing to Allah in the talbiyah." Then he came to the pass of Harsha and said: "What pass is this?" They said: "The pass of Harsha." He said: "As if I were looking at Yunus ibn Matta (peace be upon him) on a red, curly-haired she-camel, wearing a woollen cloak, the halter of her rope a palm-fibre, and he was calling out the talbiyah." Recorded by Muslim in his *Sahih* (166) and Ahmad in his *Musnad* (1/215).

7 - Al-Qurtubi cited in *al-Tadhkira* (p. 773), Dar al-Turath edition, from the hadith of Kathir ibn Abdullah from his father from his grandfather, who said: "We fought alongside the Prophet (ﷺ)…" – the hadith, in which: "The Hour will not be established until Isa ibn Maryam, the servant and messenger of Allah, descends, performing Hajj or Umrah, or Allah will gather that for him." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: a man said: "I testify that it is written in the Torah and the Gospel that he will pass by al-Rawha performing Hajj or Umrah, or Allah will gather that for him. Then Allah will make his disciples, the People of the Cave and the Inscription, pass by as pilgrims, for they have neither performed Hajj nor died."

As for the burial of the Messiah, peace be upon him, al-Qurtubi mentioned in *al-Tadhkira* (p. 762), from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "He will remain forty-five years and will be buried with me in my grave, so I and Isa will rise from one grave, between Abu Bakr and Umar." Mentioned by al-Mayanshi Abu Hafs.

And from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Isa will remain on earth after he descends for forty years, then die, and the Muslims will pray over him and bury him." Mentioned by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in his *Musnad* (hadith 2541).

8 - The verification of this matter is that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was eighty-six years old when Isma'il was born to him, by the text of the Holy Book: "Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram" (Genesis 16:16). As for his age when Ishaq was born to him, he was one hundred years old, by the text of the Book: "Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him" (Genesis 21:5). That means Isma'il was fourteen years old when his brother Ishaq was born. So how could Ishaq be his only son?

And Hagar was a wife of Ibrahim according to the text of the Torah: "So Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar her Egyptian maid, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife, and he went in to Hagar, and she conceived" (Genesis 16:3-4).

So how do they say, after these matters: "And after these things, Allah tested Ibrahim and said to him: 'O Ibrahim.' He said: 'Here I am.' He said: 'Take your son, your only son whom you love, Ishaq, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I shall tell you'" (Genesis 22:2). See (Genesis 22:6-16).

Then the Almighty says:

﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days, over the beast of cattle He has provided for them. So eat from it and feed the wretched poor man.﴾ (22:28)

The word ﴿benefits﴾ is a broad, comprehensive term that covers every kind of benefit: material and worldly, or religious and otherworldly. We should not restrict what God has made wide. Everything connected with the Hajj that belongs to the movements of life counts as a benefit. Your preparation for the Hajj, arranging its expenses, equipment and mount, contains benefits for you and for others, when you provide your family with what suffices them until you return.

Whatever buying and selling takes place in the areas of the Hajj are all mutual benefits among people: the merchant who sells to you, the owner of the house who rents it to you, and the owner of the car that transports you.

So the material benefits of the Hajj are many and interwoven, intertwined with the religious, otherworldly benefits. When you buy the sacrificial animal (hadi)(1), for example, you perform a rite and benefit the merchant who sold it to you, the breeder who raised this animal, the butcher who slaughtered it, and the poor man who ate from it.

So the Hajj is not complete except with a wide movement of life, in which there is benefit for you and for people in ways you do not know. You may look at the gifts that pilgrims bring with them for their families and relatives, especially the Egyptians among them. You will see some of them busy gathering these items before performing their rites, spending most of their time in the markets, as if they will not be a pilgrim unless they return loaded with these gifts.

For this reason some of these people used to come to us asking: "I owe a dam mut'ah(2), and I have no money. What should I do?" He wants to fast. Indeed, how will he fulfil his obligation when he has spent everything he has? So I would say to him: "Give me your travel bag, and I will sell what is in it, and I will leave you only what suffices you for expenses until you return."

Are not all of these benefits?

Among the benefits of the Hajj is that from the moment the pilgrim intends to perform this obligation and prepares himself for it, materially and spiritually, he tries to reckon his accounts anew, to correct within himself what was corrupt, to desist from what he used to commit of disobedience to God, and to set right what is between him and people. So a special process of polishing takes place in him, transforming him into a new person worthy of this great station, and fit to see the House of God and circle around it.

Among the preparations for the Hajj is that the pilgrim learns what is his and what is his duty, and adopts the etiquette of the Hajj, knowing its prohibitions and what is forbidden to him, and that he will relinquish his finery and clothes in which he takes pride, and the status he boasts of among people, and how the ihram (pilgrim garb) equalizes everyone.

He learns how to behave with himself and with all the kinds of creation around him(3). With himself, he does not think of disobedience, and his hand does not reach even to a hair of his head or a nail of his fingers, and he does not approach perfume, not even a scented soap.

Remarkably, the moment the pilgrim enters the ihram, he takes the utmost care over these rulings. I challenge anyone who intends the Hajj and begins to assume the ihram, then thinks of disobedience, because he is preparing himself for a new stage in which he purifies himself of sins. How could he acquire more of them when he has come from distant lands to be purified of them?

During the Hajj the pilgrim also behaves with courtesy toward animals: he does not hunt them or kill them, and toward plants: he does not cut down a tree. He even behaves courteously toward inanimate matter, which he regards as the lowest of the kinds of creation: he is keen to kiss the Black Stone, striving to reach it, and if he cannot, he gestures toward it with his hand.

The Hajj is a commitment and discipline that surpasses any discipline known to people of this world in the movements of their lives. In the Hajj you see this human being, the supreme master of all creatures, how humbled and submissive he is, whatever his rank. And how tranquil the human soul is when it kisses a stone while content and submissive. Indeed, a person grieves if he is unable to kiss the stone.

Then the Almighty says:﴿And that they mention the name of God on known days.﴾ (22:28)

﴿That they mention the name of God﴾: because all the acts of the Hajj are accompanied by the remembrance of God and by the talbiyah (the call "Here I am"). There is no act the pilgrim performs without his saying: "Here I am, O God, here I am." The talbiyah continues to occupy him and be his constant practice until he throws the pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqabah. The meaning of "Here I am, O God, here I am" is that the concerns of this world seek me, and You have summoned me to perform Your obligation upon me. So I answer You first, because You are my Creator and the Creator of everything that occupies me and takes me away from You.

The "known days" are the Days of Tashriq(4).

As for the meaning of ﴿over the beast of cattle He has provided for them﴾: that is, they give thanks to God for this temporary provision from which they eat and drink, and buy and sell, during the times of the Hajj. Or they give thanks to God that He created these cattle for them even if they do not perform the Hajj. In the creation of cattle, namely camels, cows, sheep and goats, and in their subjugation to man, there is profound wisdom. Beyond benefiting from their meat, milk, wool and hair, remember God and thank Him that He has subjected them to you. Had God not subjected them, you would not have been able to benefit from them. A camel, for example, this huge animal, is led by a small child, who makes it kneel and carries loads on it, whereas a human being cannot subject a serpent or a wolf, for instance.

For this reason the Exalted says: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners? And We have subjected them to them.﴾ (36:71–72)

Therefore we mention God and thank Him for the beast of cattle He has provided us, enjoying them by eating, or enjoying them by selling or as adornment, as the Exalted said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture.﴾ (16:6)

Had God not subjected them to serve you, you would not have been able to tame them and benefit from them. For this reason, it is part of God's wisdom that He leaves some of His creation untamed, and it is impossible for you in any way to make them familiar or subdue them, so that you remain mindful of this blessing and thank God for it.

We have previously given the example of the flea, which is among the lowest of these creatures; you can barely see it, yet you cannot control it, and it may disturb your sleep and keep you restless all night. You perceive this blessing in the camel that a small boy leads: if it balks at you, you cannot make it walk against its will, or if it rages, no one can control it, and it may kill its owner and attack those around it.

So you have no power over it by yourself; rather, through God's subjugation it becomes possible to benefit from it. You lead it to its slaughter, and it stands still, submissive to you.

Whoever reflects on the state of the animals that God has made lawful for us finds their matter wondrous. The animal that God has made lawful for you, you continue to benefit from throughout its life. When it is subjected to what takes its soul, what does it do? It raises its head upward and gives you the place of its slaughter, as if it were saying to you: "I am in my final moments, so strive to benefit from my flesh." People of the countryside, when they witness such a situation, say: "Seeking the lawful means slaughter." As for the animal that is not slaughtered and that God has not made lawful, it dies with its head drooping, because there is no benefit in it.

This animal, which we accuse of stupidity and say is "beast-like" and so on: if you reflected upon it, you would change your opinion. The donkey, which we take as a symbol of stupidity and lack of understanding, you drive before you, and it carries filth, and you beat it, yet it does not object to you or oppose you. If you clean it and adorn it with a silver bridle and a velvet saddle, you take it as a mount and an adornment, and it walks with you and carries you while you are on its back. If you become angry with it and use it for loads and for filth, it bears that willingly and obediently.

Look at this donkey which we take as an example of stupidity: if you want it to jump a ditch wider than its capacity and abilities, it draws back, and however much you beat it and treat it harshly, it never attempts it, because it knows the extent of its leap and knows its capability, and it does not undertake anything beyond what it can bear. And after all that, we say of it: "donkey."

Then the Almighty says:﴿So eat from it and feed the wretched poor man.﴾ (22:28)

The "wretched" (ba'is) is the one whose appearance, form and dress show that he is poor and in need. As for the "poor" (faqir), he is one whose inner state is in need, even if his outward condition appears comfortable and wealthy. These poor people are not noticed by people, and perhaps they do not know their condition and need. God has said about them: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you recognize them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently.﴾ (2:273)

The meaning is: eat from what is permissible for you to eat from, namely pure charity, or a gift to the House not conditioned on anything. That is, it is not a dam qiran or mut'ah, nor an expiation (fidyah) for violating a matter of the ihram, nor a vow (nadhr). From all of these one may not eat(7).

So: eat from charity and voluntary offerings, and likewise feed the wretched and the poor. Among God's mercy to the poor is that He made the wealthy and affluent the ones who seek out the sacrificial animals, buy them, go to the place of slaughter, and bear the hardship of all this. Then they seek out the poor to give to him while he sits in his place at rest, his provision coming to him easily and conveniently from God's bounty.

For this reason it is said: among the nobility of the poor is that God made him a pillar of the wealthy man's Islam, namely in the obligation of zakat, and He did not make the wealthy man a pillar of the poor man's Islam.

(1) Hadi: the animal sacrificed and brought to the Sacred Precinct during the Hajj (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/301). It is recommended for the pilgrim performing hajj ifrad and the performer of umrah ifrad, and obligatory for the qarin and the mutamattti', and likewise for one who has omitted an obligatory act of the Hajj such as the stoning of the jamarat or the farewell tawaf, and likewise obligatory for one who has committed a prohibited act of the ihram other than intercourse, such as using perfume or shaving. (For detailed explanation of this and the conditions of the hadi, see Sayyid Sabiq's Fiqh al-Sunnah (1/531).)

(2) Tamattu': it is performing umrah in the months of Hajj, then performing Hajj in the same year in which one performed umrah, and it is called tamattu' for the benefit of performing the two rites in the months of Hajj in one year, without returning to one's homeland. The manner of tamattu' is that one enters the state of ihram from the miqat with umrah alone, saying at the talbiyah "Here I am with umrah," performs the rites of umrah, then exits from the state of ihram and enjoys what was forbidden to him until the day of Tarwiyah arrives, when he enters ihram from Makkah for Hajj. For this, a hadi is obligatory (Fiqh al-Sunnah 1/365–366).

(3) This refers to hunting game while in a state of ihram for Hajj or umrah. The Exalted says: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram...﴾ (5:95). He also says: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers; but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram...﴾ (5:96).

(4) Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir (3/217), mentions four opinions on the interpretation of "the known days":
- The first ten days of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Mujahid and others, and it is the school of al-Shafi'i and the well-known view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
- The day of sacrifice and three days after it, which are the 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah, called the Days of Tashriq. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal adopted it in one of his narrations.
- The day of sacrifice and two days after it. This was said by Ibn Umar and al-Suddi, and it is the school of Malik.
- The day of Arafah, the day of sacrifice and the Days of Tashriq. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam, that is, the 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah.

(5) Harana al-naqah: the she-camel stood and did not move (i.e., refused to walk). It does not comply when one urges it to run; it stops (Lisan al-Arab, root h-r-n).

(6) Abu Bakr al-Jassas (d. 370 AH) said in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an, published by Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyyah (3/307): "Its apparent meaning implies the obligation to eat. However, the early scholars agree that eating from it is not obligatory. It has been narrated from Ata, al-Hasan, Ibrahim and Mujahid, who said: if he wishes he eats, and if he wishes he does not eat."

(7) Al-Jassas said in Ahkam al-Qur'an (3/307): "People differ regarding the dam of the qiran and the tamattu' into two opinions: some do not permit eating from it, and some permit eating from it but do not make it obligatory." Al-Shafi'i said in Kitab al-Umm (2/34): "The hadi is of two kinds: obligatory and voluntary. Whatever originally was obligatory upon a person, he may not withhold it, so he does not eat anything from it. This is like the hadi for corruption (of ihram), perfume, the penalty for hunting, vows, and tamattu'. If he eats from an obligatory hadi, he must give in charity the value of what he has eaten. Whatever originally was voluntary, such as sacrifices and voluntary gifts, he may eat from it, feed others, give gifts, store it, and give in charity. Yet it is more beloved to me that he does not eat it and does not withhold it, except for a third, and that he gives a third as a gift and gives a third in charity."

Then the Exalted says:

﴿Then let them complete their rites (tafath), fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.﴾ (29)

﴿Let them complete…﴾ (29): The word "qada" (قضاء) is used either for God's decree that He imposes on a person, which is a binding and necessary matter, or for a judgment by a person between disputing parties. The first task of judgment is to cut off the dispute. So the meaning of "liyaqdu" here is: let them cut off (yaqti'u).

And the meaning of ﴿tafathahum…﴾ (29): When the Qur'an was revealed with this word, it was not used in the speech of Quraysh, and it did not circulate on their tongues. So they asked the people of the desert about it, and they said: "tafath" means the grime and dirt that cling to the body. They said: "By God, we did not know it until the hour the Qur'an was revealed with it."

Therefore the meaning is: let them cut off their tafath, that is, the grime that clung to them because of their commitment to the rules of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage), where the pilgrim remains during the days of Hajj in ihram, not perfuming himself, and not taking anything from his hair or nails. When he has finished the rites of Hajj and slaughtered his sacrificial animal, it is permissible for him to cut off this tafath and remove this grime by exiting the state of ihram and doing what was forbidden to him.

As for His saying, ﴿and fulfil their vows…﴾ (29): if one has vowed something to God, he must fulfil it.

﴿And circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ (29): That is, the tawaf al-ifadah (the circumambulation of return). Tawaf means that you go around something, beginning and ending, and beginning and ending, and so on. The House has been described as "ancient" ('atiq). The word 'atiq is used in the language in wide-ranging ways, among them: old. Since it is the first house set up for mankind, it is therefore ancient, and antiquity here is a description of praise, because it means a precious thing that is guarded and cared for.

Just as we see among some people precious and rare objects that they keep and pass down, calling them "antiquities" (al-'adiyat), such as artworks and the like, and the longer time passes over them, the more their value increases and their price rises.

And 'atiq also means the beautiful and fine thing, and 'atiq also means the one freed from control and servitude to another. So what is meant by describing the House here as 'atiq?

Describing the House as ancient encompasses all these meanings: it is old, because it is the first house set up for mankind; it is costly, precious and rare, for we see in it what we do not see in other places of signs; and it is enough that seeing it and circumambulating it forgives sins; it is the House of God, which has no equal.

It is also 'atiq in the sense of freed from the control of others, because God protected it from the aggression of tyrants. Do you not see the story of the Elephant, and what God did to Abraha when he wanted to demolish it? Even the elephant that led this army realised that this was aggression against the House of God, so it turned back from the House and began to head in whatever direction they wanted except toward the Ka'bah.

It is said that a man (2) went up to the elephant and said into its ear: "Kneel, Mahmud" (the elephant's name), "and return rightly guided, for you are in the sacred land of God." The poet (3) expressed this situation, saying:

"The elephant was held back at al-Mughammas until it began to howl as if it had been wounded."(4)

Then God sent down upon them the birds in flocks (al-tayr al-ababil), which pelted them with stones until they died.

Therefore, when 'Abd al-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Messenger (ﷺ), went to speak to Abraha about the hundred camels that had been seized from his herds, Abraha said: "I was in awe of you when I saw you, but you have fallen from my esteem, since you spoke to me about a hundred camels I had taken from you, and left the House in which lies your glory and your honour."

So what did 'Abd al-Muttalib say? He said: "As for the camels, they are mine; as for the House, it has a Lord who will protect it."

Some accuse 'Abd al-Muttalib of passivity for this statement, but this is not passivity from the greatest of Quraysh; rather it is his trust in God's protection of His House. Therefore he referred the matter to One stronger than himself, as if he were saying: If I were to protect it, I would protect it by my strength, power and cunning; but I want to terrify him with God's power and might, and I did not hand over the House except while certain that the Lord of the House would protect it, and this shakes the enemy and throws him into confusion.

How similar the position of 'Abd al-Muttalib is to the position of Moses (peace be upon him), when his people said: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken (61)﴾ (al-Shu'ara'), and he said with certainty and confidence: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me (62)﴾ (al-Shu'ara').

So: 'Abd al-Muttalib was not passive, as some accuse him, but was positive in the highest sense. Had he been positive in the sense you intend, that positivity would have given him protection through his own strength; instead, his conduct, which you consider passivity, gave him protection through the power and might of God, Glorified is He. Therefore the armies of heaven intervened immediately.

But why the circumambulation and going around the Ka'bah?

They say: because the Muslim, when he is absent from the Ka'bah, prays facing its direction, each according to his location relative to it. You find Muslims in every part of the world turning towards it, each from a side: this from the north, that from the south, this from the east, that from the west, meaning in all the cardinal and intermediate directions.

When you go to the Ka'bah itself and are honoured by seeing it, do you face it from the very place you used to face in your prayer, or from another? Thus all the directions of the Ka'bah are equal for you and for others, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God (115)﴾ (al-Baqarah). There is no place more deserving than another; therefore we circumambulate the House.

1 - Al-Zajjaj said: "No one knows the meaning of al-tafath except through tafsir." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "No poetry has come in which it can be cited as evidence." Ibn al-A'rabi said regarding ﴿Then let them complete their tafath…﴾ (al-Hajj 29): "It means fulfilling their needs of shaving and cleaning" (Lisan al-'Arab, entry: tafath).
2 - He is Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami, as mentioned by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (1/52).
3 - He is Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Thaqafi.
4 - Ibn Hisham mentions this verse in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (1/60) among other verses by Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt.
5 - Ibn Hisham mentions in al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (1/39) that 'Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome, beautiful and dignified of people. When Abraha saw him, he esteemed, honoured and respected him, so as not to seat him beneath himself, and disliked that the Abyssinians should see him sitting with him on his royal throne, so Abraha came down from his throne, sat on his carpet, and seated him beside himself upon it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 22, verse 30:

Then the True One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿That. And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord. And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you. So shun the filth of idols and shun the word of falsehood.﴾

﴿That…﴾: a reference to the preceding discourse as a clear matter, but listen to a new command that is coming. Here it is a resumption of speech following earlier speech. After the discussion of the House and the rites of the Hajj connected with it, the context resumes:

﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord…﴾: God, glorified is He, wants His servant to adhere to His commands by carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. Every command of God makes it unlawful for you to abandon it, and every prohibition makes it unlawful for you to commit it. These are the sacred rites of God that you must honour by obeying the command and avoiding the prohibition.

When you honour these sacred rites, you do not honour them for their own sake, for there is nothing that has sanctity in itself. Rather, you honour them because they are the sacred rites and commands of God. Therefore, adherence to them may vary, and something may befall you that appears contradictory on the surface.

Take wudu' (ablution) for example. Some see in it the cleanliness of the body. When water runs out or is absent, tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth), by which we rub the members of tayammum, takes its place. So there is no cleanliness in the command itself; rather it is adherence, submission, and the awareness that you are approaching an extraordinary matter for which you must purify yourself with ablution. If I command you to perform tayammum, you must comply without searching for the reasons and causes of the command.

Such is the discipline in regard to commands and honouring them, because they come from God. Why not, when we see this kind of adherence, or the training of discipline in adherence, in our ordinary dealings in life? For example, when a soldier is conscripted, the first thing he learns is discipline before he holds a weapon or trains with it. He learns that the word "stand still" means not moving whatever the circumstances, so that if a scorpion stings him, he does not move.

When the instructor enters the dining hall and says "Stand still," everyone obeys. The spoon in the dish remains in the dish, and the spoon in the soldier's mouth remains in his mouth, so that in the wide hall you see not a single movement. This physical and behavioural discipline is an introduction to discipline in important and dangerous military matters afterwards.

So your Lord, mighty and majestic, is more deserving of this discipline, because worship is nothing but the discipline of a worshipper toward the commands of the One worshipped, and absolute obedience that does not admit debate. You do not perform it for its own sake but in submission to the command of God. In tawaf you kiss the Black Stone, and in stoning the jamarat you throw a pebble. This is a stone and that is a stone: this one we step on and that one we kiss. One stone is kissed and another is pelted, because the matter is one of obedience and adherence. All of this is part of honouring the sacred rites of God.

For this reason, the Imam Ali, may God be pleased with him, draws our attention to this matter when he says regarding tayammum: "If religion were a matter of opinion, the underside of the foot would be more deserving of wiping than its upper side,⁽²⁾ because filth clings first to the underside of the foot."

We have mentioned in the preceding verses that the sacred things are five: the Sacred House, the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred Land, the Sacred Monument, and the Sacred Month. The sacred rites of God are the forbidden things that you must not do.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, explains the reward of this adherence: ﴿…it is better for him with his Lord…﴾: the goodness here is not in the outward appearance of the matter or in the eyes of people, nor in the thing itself; rather, the goodness is for the servant with God.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you…﴾: You may say, how can this be, since they are lawful from the beginning and originally? They said: because the prohibition of game may lead some to think that these animals are forbidden permanently, so they would not benefit from them. Thus God made clear that they are lawful, except what has been named as forbidden, and the Qur'an stated it in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than God, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen to death, the gored to death, that which a beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered, and what is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek decision by arrows…﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3].

And His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is grave disobedience…﴾ [al-An'am 6:121].

The meaning of ﴿So shun the filth of idols…﴾: rijs (filth) is a thick impurity that penetrates the essence of a thing. That is, it is not a surface matter in it that can be removed, but it is within the thing itself, so that you cannot separate it from it.

﴿And shun…﴾: this does not indicate only abstention, but also mere approach to the causes of this disobedience. When you approach the causes and means of disobedience, it is inevitable that they will entice you and occupy your heart, and whoever hovers around a thing is about to fall into it. Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, did not say "abstain," but said "shun." We are astonished at some who have wronged themselves and say that the command "shun" does not mean the prohibition of wine, since He did not say, "wine has been forbidden to you."

We say: "shun" is more emphatic in prohibition and more comprehensive than "forbidden to you." If the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, had said, "Wine has been forbidden to you," this would mean that you do not drink it, but you may attend its gathering, press it, carry it, and sell it. But "shun" means: beware of even approaching it in any of these ways.

Therefore, you find that the Qur'anic presentation of the methodological requirements in the commands and prohibitions of God distinguishes between the limits of what God has made lawful and the limits of what He has forbidden. In commands He says: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them…﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229].

And in prohibitions He says: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not approach them…﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:187].

So regarding commands and what God has made lawful, stop at what is lawful and do not go beyond it to something else. As for prohibited things, do not come near them even by approach. When God wanted to forbid Adam and Eve from eating from the tree, He said to them: ﴿And do not approach this tree…﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35].

After the Truth, glory be to Him, commanded that the filth of idol worship be shunned, He said: ﴿And shun the word of falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 22:30]. He linked the worship of idols with the word of falsehood, as if the two were equal in sin. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) once finished the dawn prayer, then stood and said: "Beware, the false testimony has been made by God equal to idols."⁽⁴⁾

Why? Because false testimony encompasses all aspects of injustice. When a person says, "There is no god for the universe," this is false testimony, and whoever says it is a false witness. When he says, "God has a partner," this is false testimony, and whoever says it is a false witness. Likewise, when he wrongs someone, or distorts the truth, or slanders others, all of these fall under false testimony.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) enumerated the major sins, he said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Associating partners with God and disobedience to parents," and he was reclining, so he sat up and said: "Beware, and the word of falsehood, beware, and the word of falsehood." The narrator said: "He kept repeating it until we said, 'Would that he had stopped,' or until we thought he would never stop."⁽⁵⁾

They say about the false witness: "O false witness, you are the worst thing looked upon. You misled the judges and swore falsely by God."

Among the strange things about the false witness is that he is the first to fall from the eyes of people, and he falls from the eyes of the one for whose benefit he testified. Although he testified in your favour and raised your head over your adversary, your foot has trampled on his dignity and belittled him. And if he is called to testify in another case, you are the first to expose him as having testified falsely in your favour.

1 - Al-awthan (idols): plural of wathan, which is a statue of wood, iron, gold, silver, or the like. The Arabs used to set them up and worship them, and the Christians set up the cross and worship and honour it, so it is also a statue. 'Adi ibn Hatim said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a golden cross around my neck, and he said: 'Throw this idol away from you,'" meaning the cross. Its root is from wathana al-shay', meaning he stood in its place. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 6/4585).

2 - Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan (162) from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: "If religion were by opinion, the underside of the leather sock would be more deserving of wiping than its upper side. Yet I have seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ) wiping over the upper side of his leather socks." In another narration (163): "If religion were by opinion, the underside of the feet would be more deserving of wiping than their upper side."

3 - Al-munkhaniqah: an animal whose rope has wound around its neck, strangling it so that it dies. Al-mawqudhah: an animal beaten with a stick or stone until it dies before being slaughtered in the lawful manner. Al-mutaraddiyah: one that dies by falling into a pit. Al-nat*ihah: one that dies by being gored. (Al-Qamus al-Qawim).

4 - From Khuraym ibn Fatik al-Asadi, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed the dawn prayer, and when he finished, he stood and said: "The false testimony has been made equal to association with God" (three times). Then he recited this verse: ﴿So shun the filth of idols and shun the word of falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 22:30]. Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/321), al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2300), and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (3599).

5 - A hadith agreed upon, narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5976) and Muslim in his Sahih (87), from Abu Bakrah. Ibn Daqiq al-'Id said: "The Prophet's (ﷺ) concern with false testimony may be because it occurs more easily among people, and people are more careless about it, and its corruption is more easily committed, since the Muslim recoils from associating partners with God, and human nature recoils from disobedience to parents, but the inciters to the word of falsehood are many, so it is good to be concerned with it. This is not because of its greatness relative to what was mentioned with it."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿People of pure faith (ḥunafā') devoted to Allah, associating none with Him. Whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as though he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind carried him off to a faraway place.﴾ (22:31)

The verse suffices with mentioning only two of the many attributes, in summary form: being ḥunafā' (ḥanīf, plural ḥunafā', one who turns away from falsehood toward the straight path) of Allah, and not associating anything with Him. The word ḥanīf is derived from ḥanaf al-rajul, meaning the bending or inclination of a man's feet, so one says, "There is ḥanaf in him," meaning he inclines away from straightness. The description here does not mean that they are crooked; rather, what is meant is that turning away from crookedness is straightness.

For this reason Abraham, peace be upon him, was described as being ﴿a ḥanīf…﴾ (3:67, Āl ʿImrān), meaning: inclining away from the worship of idols.

We have said that heaven does not send a new message except when corruption has spread among a people, misguidance has become widespread among them, and the causes of guidance have ceased to exist, where a person has no admonisher, neither from his own self and conscience, nor from his religion, nor from his society and environment. This is because the human soul has a natural immunity to truth, but desires obscure it. When this admonisher and this immunity are absent from a society, heaven intervenes with a new prophet, a new message, and a new warning, because corruption has engulfed everyone and no one any longer admonishes another or guides him.

This is the meaning to which Allah refers in His words: ﴿They did not forbid one another from wrongdoing which they committed. Wretched indeed was what they used to do.﴾ (5:79, al-Mā'ida).

From here, Allah bore witness for the community of Muḥammad (ﷺ) that it is the best community brought forth for mankind, because the immunity to truth is established within it, and it has an admonisher from within itself who enjoins good and takes the hand of the deviant until he goes straight. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning it: "Good remains in me and in my community until the Day of Resurrection." (1)

The meaning is: the good is concentrated in me and scattered among my community. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered all the qualities of goodness, and Allah specially endowed him with perfection. But who among his community can bear the Muḥammadan perfection? Therefore Allah scattered the qualities of goodness among the whole community of Muḥammad, so each one of them took one of his attributes: this one is generous, this one is brave, this one is forbearing, and so on. His perfection (ﷺ) is thus dispersed throughout his community.

Since the community of Muḥammad has this role, he is the Seal of the Prophets, because his community will carry out his message after him. Therefore there is no need for heaven to intervene with a new message until the Hour arrives.

So we say: messengers come only at the time of crookedness; they come to straighten this crookedness and to turn from it toward uprightness. This is the meaning of ḥanīf, or ﴿ḥunafā' devoted to Allah…﴾ (22:31).

This attribute is the measure of uprightness in obeying the commands of Allah, not in obeying the commands of men. We do not set for ourselves the causes of perfection and then say: it should be such and such. Rather, the one who sets the causes of perfection for the created being is the Creator.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, does not intend that the act be done for its own sake and merely for the sake of doing it; rather He intends that the act be done because He commanded it. We have clarified this matter with the disbeliever who does good and benefits people and society, but not from the standpoint of religion and the command of Allah; rather from the standpoint of humanity, social standing, prestige, and rank among people. Such a person Allah does not deprive of his due, nor does He diminish the reward of his deed; He gives it to him in this world, in accordance with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of anyone who does good work.﴾ (18:30, al-Kahf).

But these people have no share in the reward of the Hereafter, because they worked for society, for people, and for rank; they have received their return in this world as fame, widespread renown, status, and immortality.

In the sacred ḥadīth, the Truth, glorified is He, says to them: "You did it so that it would be said, and it has been said." (2) The matter is concluded.

The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, has struck for us several examples of these people, saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; and he finds Allah with him, so He pays him in full his account. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (24:39, al-Nūr).

The deed of the disbeliever is like a mirage that appears to him from afar; one who sees it thinks there is good in it, but it is not so. When he actually confronts the matter, he finds nothing, and he is confronted with the existence of a just God whom he did not have in mind on the day he did what he did.

In another verse He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day; they have no power over anything of what they earned.﴾ (14:18, Ibrāhīm).

And He says: ﴿The likeness of one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day is like a smooth rock with a little soil on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ (2:264, al-Baqara).

Does rain produce anything when it falls upon bare, smooth rock? Thus is the deed of the disbeliever. Whoever wants the reward of the Hereafter, let him realize the meaning of ﴿ḥunafā' devoted to Allah…﴾ (22:31, al-Ḥajj): and let him act from the standpoint that Allah has commanded.

So: the deed is not done merely because it is good in itself, but because Allah has commanded you to do it. The proof is that the Lawgiver will command you to do things in which you find no good, yet you must adhere to them in order to achieve the discipline that the Wise Lawgiver intends for you; afterward the aspect of goodness in that deed will be revealed to you, and you will learn the wisdom in it.

Take as an example the position of Islam regarding the orphan. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged caring for him, honoring him, and sponsoring him, to the extent that he said: "I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be like these two in Paradise," and he pointed with his index and middle fingers. (4) So the one who sponsors an orphan is a companion of the Messenger of Allah in Paradise.

In this position there are many wisdoms, which many people may not know. The orphan has lost his father while still young; he looks around and finds no father for himself, while his companions enjoy the embrace of their fathers. If this young child does not find tenderness from all people, as though they were his fathers, a feeling of resentment toward Allah and objection to the decree that deprived him, unlike others, of a father's tenderness and care, would grow within him.

For this reason Islam wishes that the orphan be raised in a sound manner within society, neither resenting Allah nor resenting people, because they have all treated him as if he were their child.

There is another observation: when you see the standing of the orphan, and how society cares for him and raises him up, your heart will be reassured if death surprises you while your children are young. These are immunities that Islam places in society: an immunity in the orphan's soul, and an immunity in those who care for and sponsor him.

The sponsorship and honoring of the orphan must take place within the frame of ﴿ḥunafā' devoted to Allah…﴾ (22:31, al-Ḥajj): so your deed is purely for Allah, without regard to anything else of the goods of this world, unlike one who seeks guardianship of an orphan in order to benefit from his wealth, or who has an eye on his mother… etc. Such a person's deed is like what we mentioned: ﴿like a mirage in a desert plain,﴾ or ﴿like ashes upon which the wind blows violently,﴾ or ﴿like a smooth, bare rock that produces nothing.﴾

If a person tries to make his intention sincere for Allah in such a deed, he is still not safe from something mixing into it, as the noble ḥadīth says: "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness for every deed I intended for Your sake which was mixed with what was not for You." (5)

The second attribute by which Allah described His believing servants is: ﴿associating none with Him…﴾ (22:31, al-Ḥajj). Associating partners is a grave matter, because the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, as He said in the sacred ḥadīth, is the most self-sufficient of partners in need of a partner. So how can you turn to other than Allah while Allah exists?

For this reason He, glorified is He, says in the sacred ḥadīth: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners regarding partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner." (6)

Then the Truth, glorified is He, gives us an illustrative picture of the consequence of associating partners: ﴿Whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as though he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind carried him off to a faraway place.﴾ (22:31, al-Ḥajj)

Kharra (خر): means he fell from the sky with nothing holding him, and from it is His saying: ﴿So the roof fell down on them from above them…﴾ (16:26, al-Naḥl).

In man there is an inanimate aspect, because the law of gravity governs him; if he rises upward he must return to the earth by this gravity, and he cannot keep himself suspended in the air. This is a matter he does not control and is beyond his capacity. In man there is also a vegetative aspect, manifested in growth; in him there is an animal aspect, manifested in instincts; and in him there is a human aspect, manifested in reason, thought, and choosing between alternatives, and by this he is honored above the rest of creation.

You notice that kharra is connected with a great height: ﴿fell from the sky…﴾ (22:31, al-Ḥajj), such that no power can protect him or prevent him, neither by himself nor by another. Before he reaches the ground the birds snatch him away; if they do not snatch him, the wind carries him off to a distant place and plays with him. He is utterly doomed, without doubt; and any one of these three would have been sufficient.

The intelligent person should reflect on the meaning of this Qur'anic depiction and beware of this fate. This is the condition of one who associates partners with Allah. If the image is taken as a comparison of one state to another, here is the picture clearly before you. If you want another explanation that clarifies its parts: the sky is Islam, the birds are desires, and the wind is the wind of Satan, which plays with him here and there. What loss could be greater than this? And who will rescue him from this fate?

1 - Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durar al-Muntathira fi'l-Aḥadith al-Mushtahira (ḥadīth 220), where he said: "Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar said: I do not know it." Ibn Ḥajar al-Makki said in al-Fatawa al-Ḥadithiyya: "It has not come with this wording; what indicates its meaning is the well-known report: 'A group of my community will continue to be victorious upon the truth.'" Reported by al-ʿAjlūnī in Kashf al-Khafa' (1/376).

2 - From Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah say: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought forth, Allah will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. [Allah] will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I fought for You until I was martyred.' [Allah] will say: 'You lied. Rather, you fought so that it would be said, "He is brave," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, dragged on his face, and cast into the Fire." Reported by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (1905), Aḥmad in his Musnad (2/322), and al-Nasā'ī in his Sunan (6/23, 24), who also mentioned two other examples: a man who learned knowledge and taught it, and a man to whom Allah granted abundance. Shaykh al-Shaʿrawi explained it in detail in al-Aḥadith al-Qudsiyya (1/135–151).

3 - Ṣafwān: a smooth rock that is unfit for cultivation; similarly ṣaldd. Wābil: heavy rain (al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm).

4 - Reported by al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ (5304, 6005) and Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan (5150), from the narration of Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī.
